title: Ex-Cambridge professor dies week after resigning amid plagiarism allegations
summary: Jason Arday, who was Cambridge's youngest Black professor, died in London on Friday, the school said.
story: Jason Arday, who was Cambridge's youngest Black professor, died in London on Friday, a week after he resigned from the university amid plagiarism allegations, his family said. He was 41 years old.

"Jason was subjected to a campaign of sustained abuse for the more than three years since he accepted the role of Professor at Cambridge University by those who would leave no stone unturned in their quest to undermine him," his family said in a statement.

"The campaign of misinformation was too much for Jason, who was a gentle man and who always wanted to see the best in everyone. We are in shock to have lost this amazing father, partner, brother, uncle and son."

London's Metropolitan Police did not identify Arday, but said in a statement that officers responded to a report of a 41-year-old man found unresponsive inside a property at 3:12 p.m. local time Friday. Police said the man was pronounced dead at the scene and his next of kin have been notified.
His death is "unexpected, but is not believed to be suspicious," police said. The case is under investigation.
U.K. Prime Minister Andy Burnham told reporters on Saturday that Arday's death was "a tragedy on so many levels," and that it was "not a moment for any rushing to judgement."

"It's a tragedy on so many levels, but particularly just for everybody who knew Jason, his family obviously, his friends -- we think of them today," the British leader said during a visit to southwest England, according to AFP. "It's a moment for reflection, I would say, reflecting on how how things came to this."
U.K. Education Secretary Lucy Powell said in a social media post that she was "deeply shocked & saddened" to hear about Arday's death.

"My heartfelt condolences are with his friends and family at this very sad time," Powell said in the post. "I urge people to give them privacy through this incredibly difficult period & to remember there are real people with loved ones involved."

Arday resigned from Cambridge Aug. 5 following allegations of plagiarism and fabrications in his biography, saying in a statement, "The relentless accusations, speculation and public commentary have taken a profound toll on me and on those I love."
He said his resignation should not "be mistaken for an acceptance of the narratives that have surrounded me."

"We are desperately saddened to hear this tragic news. Our heartfelt sympathies go to Jason Arday's family and friends at this incredibly difficult time," Vice-Chancellor Professor at Cambridge Deborah Prentice said in a statement.

Arday joined the University of Cambridge in 2023 at age 37, becoming one of Britain's most high-profile academics after sharing an extraordinary account of his life. He said he was autistic and dyslexic, did not speak until age 11 and was unable to read or write until he was 18.

Born and raised in south London, he went to college to earn a degree in education and physical education, and then went on to earn two master's degrees before qualifying as a teacher. He then earned his Ph.D. at Liverpool John Moores University.

"Not many teachers at school had any belief in me," he told CBS News in 2023. "Educational psychologists and behavioral therapists were … very robust in their assessment that I would struggle in later life and I would need assisted living."

Allegations of plagiarism were raised last month by Nathan Cofnas, a philosopher of biology and former Cambridge researcher who has publicly criticized diversity, equity and inclusion policies. Cofnas previously wrote that in a meritocracy, "Blacks would disappear from almost all high-profile positions outside of sports and entertainment."

Arday previously denied any intentional wrongdoing, saying errors in his academic work were inadvertent and arguing that much of the criticism against him was an ideologically and racially motivated campaign against him.

Supporters of Arday also argued the scrutiny went far beyond legitimate academic criticism and said he became the target of an ideological campaign because of his work on race, inequality and diversity.
Liverpool John Moores University previously investigated allegations relating to his doctoral thesis and said it found no evidence of academic misconduct, according to The Times of London.

Articles by The Times of London and The Telegraph reported last month on possible embellishments in Arday's personal history, including claims that he raised millions for charity through endurance challenges, which he later amended. The Telegraph questioned his claim to have published a book, "Being Young, Black and Male: Challenging the Dominant Discourse," saying it could not find evidence it was ever published.
Criticism mounted ahead of this week's release of Arday's memoir, "Great and Unfortunate Things," which chronicles his life from childhood through his appointment at Cambridge.

In his resignation statement, Arday did not address the specific allegations against him, but said his resignation should not "be mistaken for an acceptance of the narratives that have surrounded me."
"It is simply the decision of someone who has reached the limits of what any person should reasonably be expected to endure," he said.

title: Paintings worth $10 million that were stolen in 3-minute heist are recovered
summary: The recovered works are valued at more than $10 million.
story: Three paintings by Renoir, Cézanne and Matisse worth millions of euros that were stolen earlier this year in a three-minute heist were recovered by Italian police.

Italian Carabinieri's art recovery squad said in a statement on Friday that the paintings were discovered during searches ordered by prosecutors in the Parma province and neighboring provinces. Five suspects were detained and they are believed to belong to an organized crime group responsible for numerous thefts of homes, businesses and other properties. Police also recovered stolen goods worth tens of thousands of euros.

The recovered artworks are Paul Cézanne's "Tasse et Plat de Cerises" ("Cup and Plate ‌of Cherries"), Pierre-Auguste Renoir's "Les Poissons" ("The Fish") and Henri Matisse's "Odalisque sur la Terrasse" ("Odalisque on the Terrace"). Art experts have valued the three paintings at more than $10 million.

The paintings were taken during a heist at the Magnani Rocca Foundation, a private museum about 12 miles from the northern city of Parma, on the night of March 22-23. Police said thieves forced open the entrance door.
Police on Friday released a video of the theft, showing two masked burglars entering through a window, grabbing the three paintings off the wall, and then immediately exiting the building.

Investigators said they retrieved important evidence at the scene, including a pickaxe and fire extinguisher with their serial numbers removed. Forensic officers were able to reconstruct the serial numbers, which linked them to an apartment building accessible to one of the alleged members of the criminal gang.
The suspects were all born in Moldova and resided in the Parma area, authorities said.

#Parma: recuperate dai #Carabinieri tre preziose opere di Paul Cezanne, Pierre Auguste Renoir, e Henri Matisse, sottratte lo scorso 23 marzo dal Museo Fondazione Magnani Rocca di Traversetolo. Valore complessivo stimato 9 milioni di euro pic.twitter.com/YYzc15MBgC
Local media reported that the thieves took the paintings in less than three minutes and escaped across the museum gardens. An alarm interrupted the theft, according to local media.
Established in 1977, the foundation hosts the collection of art historian Luigi Magnani and also includes works by Dürer, Rubens, Van Dyck, Goya and Monet.
The crime followed a series of high-profile heists at major European museums, including the theft of French crown jewels and other items from the Louvre in Paris.

The "Odalisque sur la Terrasse" was not the only Matisse painting recovered recently. Eight illustrations by the French artist that were stolen from a library in São Paulo, Brazil, last year were recovered on Thursday.

The works, with an estimated value of about $200,000, were found in a home in the town of São Bernardo do Campo, a suburb of the city, CBS News partner BBC News reported. They were stolen from the Biblioteca Mario de Andrade in December 2025. Four people have been arrested in connection with the crime.

The eight prints recovered are named "Le Clown," "Le Cirque," "Monsieur Loyal," "Cauchemar de L'Eléphant Blanc," "Le Codomas," "La Nageuse Dans L'Aquarium," "L'Avaleur de Sabres" and "Le Cowboy." They were made for an art book named "Jazz."
A total of 13 pieces of art and historical items were stolen from the library. Five works by Brazilian artist Cândido Portinari are still missing.

title: USS Washington aircraft carrier heads to Middle East to replace USS Lincoln
summary: The USS George Washington aircraft carrier departed Vietnam last week and is headed to the Middle East to replace the USS Abraham Lincoln, according to a U.S. official.
story: The USS George Washington aircraft carrier is headed to the Middle East to replace the USS Abraham Lincoln, a U.S. official tells CBS News. The Lincoln has been deployed for almost nine months and in recent weeks, some families have voiced concerns about conditions on the ship, including supply shortages and mental health issues.

During a town hall with the acting Navy secretary last week, some families expressed frustration that he offered no update about when the carrier would come home. But the Navy does not usually publicly announce the exact timing of a carrier's movements in order to protect the ship's security. The USS Lincoln deployed in November 2025, first to the Pacific but then was sent to the Middle East ahead of the Iran war.
Navy Secretary Hung Cao wrote on X that the Lincoln "will return home soon as part of a planned rotation."
The Wall Street Journal first reported the USS Washington would replace the USS Lincoln in the Middle East.

At least one spouse during the town hall voiced concerns about the mental well-being of her partner, according to a person familiar with the events. Media reports this week quoted some family members who said they had heard multiple sailors had thought about jumping overboard.

The Navy pushed back on the notion that there is a mental health crisis onboard. In a statement to CBS News, a Navy spokesperson said, "We have not identified an increase in reported suicidal ideation or suicide attempts aboard the ship. We take every service member's well-being seriously and have religious, medical and mental health professionals available to assess and address concerns as they arise."
A Navy official told CBS News there has been a decrease in suicidal ideation cases as the deployment has gone on.

There is an incident of a sailor going overboard earlier this month that is being investigated, according to the Navy. The sailor was rescued safely and left the ship for follow-on care. The circumstances of how and why the sailor fell overboard are unclear and part of the investigation.

A U.S. official also confirmed Friday that in April, a sailor fell off the USS Frank E. Petersen destroyer, which is part of the Lincoln carrier strike group. The sailor was immediately recovered and received care. There are occasionally sailors who go overboard accidentally. CBS News has asked the Navy for comment. CNN first reported that a sailor had gone overboard from the Lincoln strike group in April.
In a post on social media, Cao acknowledged that "a small number of mental health cases were treated with no loss of life."

A Navy official told CBS News on Friday the military is sending additional social workers and counselors to the Lincoln "to augment the already robust mental health resources available to the crew 24/7."

Meanwhile, one spouse of a service member on the Lincoln told CBS News that earlier in the deployment, the sailors experienced some food shortages while they waited for resupply, but that has been resolved.
The Navy in a statement acknowledged some delays for other items. The ship is "in a highly contested environment where traditional supply hubs in the Middle East were disrupted by combat actions."

"In response, leadership prioritized mission-critical supplies: first food, then hygiene items, then mail," the statement said. "Current reports from the ship confirm continuous access to clean water, functional [air conditioning] and healthy meal options."
Democrats have pressed the Pentagon for more information about the conditions on the ship.

"When a member of the military raises their right hand, they know they're going to endure some hardship. But they should expect that our leaders should do everything possible to avoid additional hardship, not contribute to the hardship," Democratic Sen. Richard Blumenthal of Connecticut told CBS News' "The Takeout with Major Garrett," calling conditions aboard the Lincoln "abhorrent."
Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth told reporters Thursday that some of the reporting was "completely misrepresented."

"We make sure that every ship, every crew, every captain has everything we can provide them at every single moment," Hegseth said. "Some deployments are longer than others, and I have more respect and gratitude for those sailors than anybody."

Cao also argued Friday the situation aboard the Lincoln has been misrepresented, writing that "our young men and women have been pushed to their limits—but they have never broken." He said "meal plans were adjusted when fresh resupply was unavailable, without a single meal being missed."

The Japan-based USS George Washington left port in Yokosuka in May for a Pacific patrol and was seen this week moving west through the Strait of Malacca. Once in the Middle East, it will join the USS George H.W. Bush carrier and leave the U.S. without a carrier in the Pacific.

title: Liechtenstein moves to change succession laws, paves way for women on throne
summary: The change shouldn't affect the top of the line of Liechtenstein's royal house succession in the immediate future.
story: Liechtenstein's royal house said Saturday that the tiny country's rules of succession will be changed so that a woman could inherit the principality's throne in the future.

Hereditary Prince Alois announced the change in his speech marking the country's national day. He said it was approved on Wednesday by the necessary two-thirds majority of family members who can vote on such matters.

The prince said, according to a text of his remarks posted on the princely house's website, the vote allowed that "all female descendants of the Princely House will be granted the same participation rights in matters governed by the House Law as male descendants."

"The line of succession will be adjusted from male primogeniture to absolute primogeniture," Alois said. "That means that in the future, the first-born child will, regardless of sex, become the heir to the throne and later the princess or prince of Liechtenstein."
The change shouldn't affect the top of the line of succession in the immediate future.

Prince Hans-Adam II remains the head of state, but in 2004 handed over most of his powers to Alois, his eldest son, who is now 58. That was in line with a tradition of Liechtenstein monarchs giving up the reins to their heirs.
The eldest of Alois' four children is 31-year-old Prince Joseph Wenzel.

Liechtenstein, a wealthy nation of 40,000 people that borders Switzerland and Austria, has an unusually powerful monarchy by European standards. The ruling prince has the power to veto referendum results, appoint judges and fire the government.

The country is traditionally conservative and in 1984 became the last European country to grant women the right to vote in national elections. Male voters narrowly approved the change, which Hans-Adam had backed, in a referendum.
Last year, Brigitte Haas became its first female prime minister.

title: Father and young sons rescued after 16 hours stranded off Thai island
summary: The father and his two sons had rented a jet ski from a local operator, but failed to return it at the agreed time.
story: A French family was rescued after their jet ski capsized off the coast of Thailand's Koh Samui, leaving them stranded for over 16 hours.

The father, 50, and his two sons, 5 and 7, rented the jet ski from a local operator on Koh Samui, a Thai resort island, around 5 p.m. local time Thursday. After the family failed to return at the set time, the operator informed local rescuers and authorities, local government official Amorn Chomchoey told AFP.

The report spurred a frantic search for the three. The Bangkok Post reported that searchers used speedboats and more jet skis to comb the waters. Search efforts were suspended overnight, then resumed in the morning. The family was found around 10 a.m. local time on Friday.

Footage of the rescue shared by the Koh Samui district office and the BBC showed the jet ski almost completely capsized, with only its triangular front section visible above the water. One of the boys was sitting on top of the jet ski while his father floated nearby, both of them wearing life jackets.
One rescuer can be heard shouting, "Calm down" and "They survived," and later helped the boy onto another boat. Video shows rescuers providing the family with water.

Chomchoey said the father and sons were "pale" and "exhausted after swallowing a lot of seawater," but otherwise well, according to CBS News partner BBC. The three family members were taken to an area hospital for checks and discharged shortly afterward, Chomchoey said.
The BBC reported that the boys' mother and older sister had been waiting on the beach. The reunited family is continuing its holiday, the BBC reported.

Investigators are looking into why the jet ski capsized after operating for just 15 minutes. The father said rough waves had struck the jet ski, causing its engine to stop, the Bangkok Post reported. The BBC reported that the father described himself as an experienced jet ski driver.
The jet ski operator told other local media that the family appeared to have traveled outside the area specified by the rental agreement for the jet ski.
Koh Samui is one of Thailand's most popular islands for families, thanks to its calm seas and wide range of resorts, attracting millions of visitors each year.

title: Construction workers find $10 million gold stash in renovations
summary: Police issued a warning telling "gold prospectors" to stay away from the construction site
story: Construction workers in Belgium stumbled upon a stash of gold believed to be worth more than $10 million during renovation work on a building.

Police said they were "immediately" contacted by the workers after they discovered "a large quantity of gold" while working on a building in the east Flemish town of Dendermonde. The local police department posted a picture on its Facebook page of around 50 gold bars and piles of gold coins.

Belgian news outlets reported that bars and coins worth an estimated nine million euros ($10.4 million) were found bricked into the cellar walls during the renovation of a house belonging to a local charity, CAW East-Flanders.
One worker interviewed by Belgian news outlet VRT said the crew's "first reaction was actually disbelief, amazement."
"We stumbled across it while carrying out groundwork to lay a pipe for the sewerage system," said the man identified only as Kobe. "We certainly hadn't expected to find gold."
Police said the gold was "inventoried and secured as quickly as possible in a high-security vault belonging to the federal government services."

"Apparently, several treasure hunters would like to pay another visit to the site," read a Facebook post by the police department -- which changed its profile picture to a gold coin in light of the find.
"A golden piece of advice: it is truly pointless," they said -- cautioning the curious to stay away from the fenced-off construction site.
It was not clear who was considered the legal owner of the trove -- and if anyone would get to keep it.
"Let us hope that this treasure ends up in the right hands," said the police post.

title: Russian tanker leaking oil off Oman coast, threatening environmental disaster
summary: The Caroline Bezengi, linked to Russia's so-called shadow fleet, is carrying millions of gallons of oil and has run aground off the coast of Oman.
story: A Russian tanker carrying millions of gallons of oil has run aground off the coast of Oman — and now risks breaking apart, potentially causing an environmental disaster on the scale of the 1989 Exxon Valdez spill.

The Caroline Bezengi, which has been linked to Russia's so-called shadow fleet to move sanctioned oil around the world, was damaged by an unexplained explosion on June 8. The tanker had departed Russia, traveled through the Suez Canal and entered the Gulf of Oman when its crew abandoned ship, according to John Amos, whose environmental nonprofit SkyTruth has been tracking the ship for weeks. Left adrift, it eventually grounded on a rocky outcropping near a small, uninhabited island.

Satellite images showed the first signs of an oil leak on June 30, Amos said. He estimates that hundreds of thousands of gallons had spilled by Aug. 7. Five of the tanker's six cargo holds were filled with oil, Amos said, meaning the vessel could have been carrying as much as 40 million gallons.

The ship's owner has given no public indication that it is responding to the accident, and the tanker may not have adequate insurance. That has left Oman with responsibility for containing the spill and preventing a far larger disaster. The government has deployed aircraft, divers and specialized personnel to assess the vessel and prepare mitigation efforts, according to Greenpeace.

Ambrey, a British maritime security and salvage company, says crews are on their way to the tanker. But they will face what the company described as "extreme adverse weather and sea conditions influencing vessel stability" as monsoon storms batter the region.

Safely removing the remaining oil will require a complex operation, and according to Hanen Keskes, regional campaigns lead at Greenpeace MENA, the full extent of the leak may not be known until that work is completed.

The environmental stakes are considerable. The Gulf of Oman and the Arabian Sea are home to protected marine life, including sea turtles, sharks and a rare population of humpback whales. The waters surrounding the grounded tanker were also recently designated a marine reserve.

Russia relies on hundreds of aging tankers in its shadow fleet. The vessels often operate through opaque ownership structures and may carry little or no credible insurance, raising questions about who will ultimately pay for the salvage operation and environmental cleanup.
Amos warns that even a rapid response can recover only a fraction of the oil released into the sea.
"Once the oil hits the water, you've already lost," he said, estimating that spill-response efforts typically recover only about 20%.

The potential cost is enormous. Exxon spent approximately $2.1 billion after at least 11 million gallons of oil spilled from Exxon Valdez off Alaska's coast in 1989 — roughly $5.8 billion in today's dollars.

story: Rookie professional golfer Jessica Bang of Australia died in a hospital in Thailand on Thursday at the age of 18, the WPGA Tour of Australasia said. She died after suffering a brain hemorrhage, BBC Sport reported.
Bang collapsed on Aug. 1 as she was preparing in Thailand for a tournament and was transported to a hospital in Bangkok, where she underwent emergency brain surgery.

The "Australian golf community is deeply saddened by the passing of young tour member Jessica Bang in Thailand," the WPGA Tour of Australasia said in a statement. "Jessica was an outstanding young talent who made a significant impression in her short time on the tour."
A GoFundMe page that was set up by Bang's cousins has raised more than $50,000 AUD.

"As her cousins, we will forever cherish the time and memories we shared with Jessica," they wrote on the page. "Her sense of humour, together with her cheerful and vibrant personality, will always be remembered and treasured by our family.

Bang earned her place on the tour through qualifying school at the end of last year,  and won the Women's New South Wales Open Regional Qualifying Event in February in just her fifth professional start. According to BBC Sport, she shot a final-round 65 to win the event to reach the NWS Women's Open on the Ladies European Tour, where she missed the cut.

title: Count Binface wins hearts, if not the election, in bid to defeat Trump ally
summary: Count Binface, a satirical candidate who's become a mainstay in recent U.K. elections, achieved his greatest success yet.
story: Count Binface may have come up short in the by-election against Nigel Farage, but don't throw his popularity in the trash just yet. The candidate wearing a garbage can on his head just won over a quarter of the votes in a contest against one of Britain's most famous politicians.
The longtime satirical candidate had his best showing yet in a surreal campaign triggered by Farage's own resignation.
Binface has a simple message to voters: "I'm here to take out the trash." (In the U.K., a trash can is called a bin, though, so his name might go over some Americans' heads.)
A mainstay of British politics, Binface has been on the ballot in several elections over the past few years.

The man behind the trash can is satirist Jonathan Harvey, and Binface continues a long tradition of quirky political candidates in U.K. elections. After all, a musician named Screaming Lord Sutch, founder of the Official Monster Raving Loony Party, holds the record for running in the most parliamentary elections: 39 votes spanning from the 1960s to the '90s.

First, adopting the garb of a prior novelty candidate, Binface ran as Lord Buckethead against then-U.K. Prime Minister Theresa May. Then, he adopted the moniker of Count Binface, competing against the likes of Boris Johnson and, most recently, current U.K. Prime Minister Andy Burnham.
He, of course, lost all those races, and received very few votes. This is the first time he crossed the 5% threshold that earns him back his 500-pound (about $677) deposit to run.

Following his defeat, Binface will not be able to implement his sweeping and, some might say, radical electoral agenda, which included nationalizing Adele, cutting your taxes while raising everyone else's and building "at least one affordable house."
The election featured a record 34 candidates, which created a comically long paper ballot, with the Reform U.K. Party's Farage taking about 63% of the votes.
But still, there was a marked difference in Binface's candidacy this time, where he won 9,455 votes, or about 27%. He secured just 95 votes in his challenge to Burnham.

Thursday's election itself was a bit of a farce though so maybe the satirical candidate was the perfect foil for Farage. An ally of President Trump who has led a surging far-right, populist movement in the U.K., Farage resigned in early July as a lawmaker to trigger the special election.
"I've decided that the people of Clacton should be the judges of my actions," Farage said when he announced his resignation.
"This will be a people versus the establishment by-election," he said, calling it "a chance to stick two fingers up to the entire establishment to frankly tell them where to go."

The move was thought at the time to be a high-risk political gamble to renew his mandate from voters as he faced mounting pressure over a scandal connected to failing to disclose financial gifts. But Binface's candidacy became more viable when every legitimate party boycotted the election.

Farage's reelection now makes him a serious threat to Burnham in the next national elections. Those elections must be called by August 2029, but a prime minister can also call for them at any time before then. Most recently, Prime Minister Keir Starmer resigned after he lost the support of many within his party, and fellow Labour Party member Burnham was chosen to replace him.
Of course, a surging Count Binface would also be a natural to run in 2029 as well.

title: Warship that sank in 1908 found off U.K.: "Undisturbed for 118 years"
summary: The Royal Navy and shipwreck hunters have been searching in vain for the remains of HMS Tiger for over a century.
story: A long-lost naval ship that sank more than a century ago off England has been located by divers exploring the waters off the Isle of Wight, military officials and an exploration team confirmed this week.

In 1908, the 400-ton HMS Tiger, a torpedo boat destroyer, collided with the 10,000-ton cruiser HMS Berwick during the night, slicing her in two, according to the Royal Navy. The Tiger's bow sank instantly and its smashed stern sank minutes later, killing more than half of the 57 crewmembers on board.

The tragedy made front-page news, with one newspaper headline saying the ship was "crushed as an eggshell." King Edward VII sent a telegram of sympathy and postcards were made to commemorate the lost sailors.

The Royal Navy and shipwreck hunters have been searching in vain for the remains of HMS Tiger for over a century. Finally, a dive team called ProjectXplore was able to pinpoint the wreck's location after spending five years piecing together archival data.

The dive team said the discovery of the stern engine revolution telegraph and the rudder position indicator revealed that the ship did not change direction nor reduce its speed before colliding with the much bigger HMS Berwick.

"Our recent exploratory project at the HMS Tiger site yielded compelling evidence regarding the final moments leading to the collision, preserving details that have remained undisturbed for 118 years," ProjectXplore wrote in a social media post, showing images of the sunken instruments.
A report on the expedition also reveals the team found numerous other relics from the vessel, including a compass, torpedo tubes, guns, ammunition, an anchor and the ship's bell.
The team also found the wreck of cruiser HMS Nottingham in the North Sea last year, BBC News reported.
Under new legislation, potentially thousands of shipwrecks, such as HMS Tiger, will be safeguarded from the moment they are found by a "protected place" designation, the Royal Navy said.
Leo Fielding and Dan McMullen, co-organizers of ProjectXplore, praised the new legislation.

"It has been the privilege of a lifetime to research, discover and document the wreck of HMS Tiger," they said. "We sincerely hope that our work will ensure that HMS Tiger, her story and the memory of those connected with her endure for future generations."

title: French teen social media ban struck down by top constitutional authority
summary: France's social media ban, which was due to take effect on Sept. 1, would have barred younger users from networks such as TikTok, Snapchat and Instagram.
story: France's top constitutional authority on Friday struck down a ban on social media access for children under 15, dealing a blow to the legislation championed by President Emmanuel Macron.

The Constitutional Council found that Article 1 of the legislation "constitutes an infringement that is neither appropriate, necessary, nor proportionate" to the freedom of expression and communication of those under 15.
In its ruling, the Constitutional Council also expressed concern about the potential impact on privacy of introducing an age-verification system for all users.
The law, which was due to take effect on Sept. 1, would have barred younger users from social networks such as TikTok, Snapchat and Instagram, among other restrictions.

The French government had promoted the ban as a way to better protect young people from the harmful effects associated with social media platforms, including anxiety, depression, sleep disorders and online harassment.
Macron had in July thanked members of Parliament for backing the legislation and pledged to enforce it by September.
After the ruling, the Elysee Palace said Macron had tasked Prime Minister Sebastien Lecornu with working on a new "legally robust draft" of the legislation.
Lecornu will have to work "as quickly as possible" on a draft that takes into account both the Constitutional Council's ruling and the European regulatory framework, the palace said.
The presidency said Macron's determination to see the reform implemented remained undiminished.

Macron has made online child safety a defining issue of the final years of his presidency, and a new ban could be one of the last major domestic reforms he ushers through. Macron will mark a decade in office next year, and he cannot run again in April's national election as, like the U.S., France has a two consecutive term limit for its presidents.
Following Friday's ruling, Macron's former prime minister, Gabriel Attal, who backed the proposal, expressed his disappointment.
"We take note of it and respect this decision, which applies to everyone," he said on social media, vowing to continue fighting against what he described as "a deadly poison for our children."

The Constitutional Council did not rule on a separate provision banning mobile phone use in high schools starting Sept. 1. Students are already prohibited from having phones in French elementary and middle schools.
A growing number of countries are taking steps to restrict social media access amid increasing warnings over its harmful effects on children.

title: Dad of USS Lincoln sailor worries about crew as deployment stretches on
summary: The USS Abraham Lincoln has been at sea for nine months, and sailors have maintained a grueling pace amid the war in Iran.
story: The father of a sailor aboard the USS Abraham Lincoln said he's worried for his son and the rest of the ship's crew as the aircraft carrier's deployment to the Middle East stretches on.

The ship has been at sea for nine months, much longer than the typical deployment of six months. Combat aircraft have launched from the carrier more than 10,000 times in the past eight months, U.S. officials say. Meanwhile, the 5,000 sailors and Marines on board the carrier have had to defend against Iranian missiles and drones. Family members say they worry about conditions aboard the ship, and fear the long deployment and grueling pace are worsening mental health issues.

"They should not be deployed this long," said Jefferson Kelley, whose son Jackson is aboard the Lincoln on his first-ever deployment. "These are old ships. It's not like they're even state-of-the-art. And they take a lot of maintenance, a lot of work. It's around the clock."

Elected officials have demanded answers about the conditions aboard the vessel. Sen. Richard Blumenthal sent a letter to Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, citing "widespread reports of shortages of basic supplies, water contamination, plumbing issues ... and deteriorating mental health."

U.S. Central Command says reports of increased suicidal ideation among the crew are false, and said there have been no deaths aboard the vessel. The circumstances of an incident on Aug. 3 where a sailor fell overboard and was recovered remain under investigation, according to a Navy statement.

The U.S. Navy said in a statement that sailors aboard the ship have access to clean water, air conditioning and healthy meal options, even as "traditional supply hubs in the Middle East were disrupted by combat actions." Hegseth said this week that reports of poor conditions aboard the carrier are "completely misrepresented," and that he has "more respect and gratitude for those sailors than anybody."

CENTCOM noted the ship has one of the highest crew reenlistment rates of the carriers in the U.S. Navy, and said the sailors and Marines aboard "remain resilient and resolved after more than 260 days at sea." The Navy also said it "has not identified an increase in reported suicidal ideation or suicide attempts aboard the ship," and noted that crew members are being provided with resources including counselors, chaplains and medical professionals.

Still, Kelley said he fears he can't trust what he's hearing from officials. Sailors' families relayed their concerns directly to the Navy's acting secretary, Hung Cao, in a contentious meeting last week. Family members including Kelley have also written letters to officials voicing their concerns. Kelley said in his message, he begged officials to find any way to send his son home, even offering to volunteer in his place.

"What's going through my mind as a parent is that need to want to be there, to want to be there for your child," Kelley said. "I would get on a plane or helicopter tonight to get shipped out to the Lincoln if it meant bringing him home to his mom and his siblings and his family."

There may be some relief in sight. The USS George Washington aircraft carrier departed Vietnam last week and is headed to the Middle East to replace the USS Abraham Lincoln, a U.S. official told CBS News. However, there is usually an overlap in carrier rotations, meaning it may still be weeks before the Lincoln returns to its home port in San Diego. The Washington's movements also leave a gap in the Indo-Pacific region, including China, for the first time since 2024.

title: What Taylor Sheridan's biggest stars really think about working with the 'Yellowstone' creator
summary: Zoe Saldaña, Billy Bob Thornton, Harrison Ford and Kevin Costner reveal what it's really like working with Taylor Sheridan on his hit shows.
story: Billy Bob Thornton told Fox News Digital that Taylor Sheridan's "Landman" is a worldwide phenomenon.
The third season of Taylor Sheridan's hit show "Lioness" has officially begun.

"Lioness" is one of many successful shows created by the prolific TV writer and showrunner. His long list of credits also include, "Yellowstone," "1923," "Landman," "The Madison" and many other popular shows.
It's not only audiences who have fallen in love with the complex characters and storylines Sheridan has created, but also the actors who work on his sets.
Here is what some of his stars have said about what it's really like to work with Sheridan.
ZOE SALDANA SAYS TAYLOR SHERIDAN GIVES STARS TWO CHOICES: 'MAKE SURE THAT YOU DON'T F--K UP... OR YOU QUIT'
Sheridan's actors have all spoken about his abilities as a writer. (Omar Vega/Getty Images)
Michael Kelly
Kelly called Sheridan "one of the greatest storytellers in history." (TheStewartofNY/FilmMagic)
Ahead of the season three premiere of "Lioness," one of its stars, Michael Kelly, told People that Sheridan is "truly a standalone talent."
"There’s nobody who’s doing or has ever done what he’s doing," he said. "It’s incredible what he does. And he’s just one of the smartest dudes you’ll ever meet."
He added, "He’s f---ing brilliant, man. Brilliant. And just one of the greatest storytellers."

When it comes to working with the showrunner in the future, Kelly said that while he's "never thought about how the shows could cross over," he has told Sheridan, "anything you want me to do, I'll do."
He told Sheridan, "I love being in Texas. I love saying your words," and that "Anything, dude. You can put me in. Put me in, coach. Wherever you want to put me, I’ll go."
Zoe Saldaña

Zoe Saldaña opened up about working with Taylor Sheridan, saying the "Lioness" creator challenges actors while remaining collaborative on set. (Dia Dipasupil/WireImage/Getty Images; Phillip Faraone/Getty Images for Viacom/Getty Images)

Actress Zoe Saldaña has starred in all three seasons of "Lioness," and told "CBS Mornings" that while she can "feel like an old soldier" on set, when Sheridan shows he believes in her, "you have no other choice but to start believing in yourself again."
The actress also referred to him as "an intimidating cat," who comes to set ready and "so serious," noting, "it raises the bar for the rest of us."

"So working with him is a challenge in the sense that he does raise the bar," Saldaña also told People. "And you have one of two choices. You either accept the challenge and make sure that you don't f--- up... or you quit."
Zoe Saldaña plays the role of Joe in "Lioness." (Lauren Smith/Paramount+)

She added that one of the benefits of working with Sheridan is that "he's an incredibly smart person" who puts in a ton of research when writing his scripts, "And then he writes these incredibly elaborate shows that end up really educating us as well."
"It's actually great," she added. "When you work with him is when you realize how passionate he is about actors and about acting. I think it is his first love when it comes to the arts."
Billy Bob Thornton
Thornton said he loves working with Sheridan on "Landman." (Scott Dudelson/Getty Images for Stagecoach)
When speaking at a Q&A in Hollywood in April, "Landman" star Billy Bob Thornton told the crowd that he has a lot of trust in the show, noting, "I trust Taylor and I trust the castmates."
"Yeah, oh, it’s great. I love working with Taylor," Thornton said, per People. "I love hanging out with him after hours. He’s such a brilliant guy, great writer, and I love his company."
Michelle Pfeiffer
Pfeiffer checked with Helen Mirren before accepting the role in Sheridan's show, "The Madison." (Steve Granitz/FilmMagic)
When speaking with The Hollywood Reporter in March, Michelle Pfeiffer spoke about how Sheridan convinced her to star in "The Madison."

"[Taylor] wanted to know who Stacy was before he started writing. I wanted to know who Stacy is before I committed. And so we went back and forth like that for a little while, and it became clear to me I wasn’t going to win this battle," Pfeiffer said. "So I asked Helen Mirren [who previously starred in Sheridan's "Yellowstone" spin-off "1923"] to speak to me about her experience."

"And she just glowed; she couldn’t say enough nice things," Pfeiffer recalled of Mirren. "She said the scripts were great, the productions were perfect. She was having the time of her life; she loved Montana. So I took a big leap of faith, and I committed. I thought, 'Well, the guy has a pretty darn good track record.'"
Harrison Ford
Ford called Sheridan an incredible writer and an intellectual. (John Sciulli/The Hollywood Reporter via Getty Images)

Harrison Ford starred in Sheridan's "Yellowstone" prequel series, "1923," and had nothing but nice things to say about the showrunner when speaking about him at the premiere of the show in December 2022.
"He’s an incredible horseman. He’s a genuine athlete, and that’s something you might not expect to find in such a talented writer and intellectual thinker," he told The Hollywood Reporter.
Kevin Costner
Costner told Entertainment Weekly that Sheridan is "doing special work." (Getty Images)

Ahead of the release of his movie "Horizon: An American Saga" in 2024, Kevin Costner spoke with Entertainment Weekly about working with Sheridan, as his future on "Yellowstone" was uncertain at the time.
The actor told the outlet that Sheridan is "doing special work in a lot of different ways."

"He's very prolific about the things he does, and if he sees me in something that he wants to do, I'll look at it just the way I did 'Yellowstone' and maybe we will end up doing something together," Costner says. "He likes a lot of the things that I like, and the idea of us working together is not out of the question for me."

He went on to say that "the subjects he chooses are very interesting to me," and that, aside from "Yellowstone," "other things that he's doing, I think, are really, really good. He likes the same subjects that I do."
Costner ultimately didn't return to film the last episodes of "Yellowstone." (Kevin Mazur/Getty Images for Airbnb)

Costner ultimately did not return to film the remainder of "Yellowstone" season five. A new spin-off, "Dutton Ranch," continued the Dutton family's story and followed Cole Hauser and Kelly Reilly's characters as they left Montana to start a new life in Texas.
Helen Mirren
Mirren starred in the "Yellowstone" spin-off series "1923." (Karwai Tang/WireImage; Emerson Miller/Paramount+)
Helen Mirren spoke to The Hollywood Reporter in December 2022 at the premiere of "1923."
When speaking with the outlet, she gave fans an inside look at what it's like working with Sheridan, calling him "fabulously hands-off."

"He presents the script, and it’s so extraordinary that you don’t want to change a word. You want to do it exactly as it’s written because it’s written with incredible precision but without being labored," she said. "To be able to be a part of a franchise in a world that is so singular on American television is very exciting. There’s nothing else quite like it."
Brian Geraghty
Geraghty praised Sheraton for his writing and casting ability. (Valerie Terranova/Getty Images for Searchlight Pictures)
"1923" star Brian Geraghty spoke with The Hollywood Reporter at the premiere of the show in December 2022 about his experience working with Sheridan.
Geraghty explained that he "expected someone totally different" prior to meeting Sheridan for the first time, and how his experience as an actor makes him a great showrunner.
'LANDMAN' STAR MICHELLE RANDOLPH STUNS IN BARELY-THERE METALLIC YELLOW BIKINI IN NEW SUMMER PHOTO DUMP

"He told me great stories of his time as an actor, about the process and how he hired some of the younger actors on the show by giving them a break over some really big-name actors," he said. "I love that because we all need that break. I got it 15 or 20 years ago and a few of the actors on the show got that from him."
He explained that his experience as an actor makes him "really empathetic to actor," although he presents as "this tough cowboy."
Geraghty starred in the "Yellowstone" spin-off, "1923." (Rodin Eckenroth/WireImage)

"I think he casts really well, and he does not care what you have done, for the most part. He casts the people who are right for the role," he explained. "When you show up to work, everyone raises the bar. He creates that, and it starts from him, but he also is very welcoming and gives you the tools you need to get there."
Michelle Randolph
Michelle Randolph played Elizabeth Strafford in "1923." (James Minchin III/Paramount+)
Michelle Randolph, who has appeared in both "1923" and "Landman," echoed Geraghty's statement and credited Sheridan for being willing to give unknown actors a break.

When speaking to People in 2025, Randolph praised Sheridan as "one of the few people" in the business who "takes chances on actors" and who "has given us this opportunity, and I just am eternally grateful for him."
"He made my dreams come true. I tell him that every time I see him," Randolph said. "He's like, 'Michelle, stop. I get it.' I'm like, 'Thank you.' But he really did give us something."

In addition to praising his casting methods, Randolph also complimented him as a writer, telling The Hollywood Reporter in December 2022 that he gives his characters "such depth and such unique storylines."
Randolph credits Sheridan for changing her life by taking a chance on her as an actress. (Gilbert Flores/WWD via Getty Images)

"No matter how many different situations are going on at once," she said. "Every character is so uniquely themselves and that’s really hard to do as a writer, especially for the amount of shows that he’s writing for."
Kurt Russell
Russell said "The Madison" is Sheridan's best writing. (Gilbert Flores/Variety via Getty Images)
Kurt Russell could not help but praise Sheridan's writing ability while at the premiere of "The Madison" in March.

"I love his writing. I think this is his best writing. I love that this is not 'Yellowstone.' It's not that. It's very It's very standalone, very different," he told Page Six. "I love the relationships that he digs into here. And I think that this is truly a different wheelhouse for him. It was fun to do."
CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR THE ENTERTAINMENT NEWSLETTER
Ali Larter
Larter, who plays Angela in "Landman," revealed she knew Sheridan prior to being cast on the show but hadn't spoken to him in a decade. (Emerson Miller/Paramount+)
Ali Larter has developed a close friendship with Sheridan through working with him on "Landman."
When speaking with People in April, Larter shared that Sheridan will often text her as he is writing, saying "if he’s laughing at his own writing… I’ll get a text."

"I mean, you know, the first season, I spent a ton of time with Taylor," she said. "He has a very clear vision of what he wants… and he is a visionary because when he is writing the scripts, he knows how he’s going to edit them."
LIKE WHAT YOU'RE READING? CLICK HERE FOR MORE ENTERTAINMENT NEWS
She went on to say that, as actors, they often "want to advocate for your character," but Sheridan is "brilliant" at creating a world "where that fits into the story that he wants to tell."
Larter credited Sheridan for being an amazing writer. (Emerson Miller/Paramount+)
Larter also praised his writing ability and work ethic when speaking with Taste of Country, calling him "the best working writer."
"He's brilliant at the way he crafts his stories," she said. "I love the characters he creates, because they're dynamic and powerful ... But he also has space to show their vulnerable sides."

When speaking with The Hollywood Reporter in June, Larter shared that she and Sheridan knew one another prior to her getting cast in "Landman," but that they hadn't spoken in over a decade when she was cast on the show.
Larter called Sheridan "an extraordinarily hard worker." (GC Images)

"I don’t think that you can pin him down," she told the outlet. "I think that he’s not going to come back into the machine that just wants to break him down. And he wants to work. He’s an extraordinarily hard worker. He’s a brilliant talent. He wants to do it his way. And I think that it’s very hard in our industry to do things your own way when you’re part of the machine."

title: Jessica Simpson turns heads in bikini photos from trip to Turks and Caicos
summary: Jessica Simpson shared bikini photos from her Turks and Caicos birthday trip on Instagram, lounging in a black polka dot two-piece in paradise.

Simpson celebrated eight years of sobriety in November 2025. (Kevin Mazur/Getty Images for JS)

title: Henry Winkler opens up about the unexpected career he considered before becoming an actor
summary: Henry Winkler almost studied to become a child psychologist before transitioning into a career as an actor and finding fame as Fonzie on "Happy Days."
story: Henry Winkler says he formed a friendship with Adam Sandler after he called to thank him for including him in his 'Chanukah Song.’
Henry Winkler is opening up about what career path he would have chosen had he not gotten into acting.

During a recent interview on the "You Could Make This Beautiful" podcast, the 80-year-old actor shared that he almost decided to become a child psychologist, because he was so dyslexic that "whatever I could do, with the least amount of education" was what he wanted to do.

"I understand children. I’m able to listen, I think, to children. I’m interested in what they have to say and how they are. I marvel at their prowess in the universe," Winkler said. "Yes, I would work with children."
Ultimately, the actor found fame playing Arthur "Fonzie" Fonzarelli on "Happy Days" from 1974 to 1984, a role which earned him three Emmy Award nominations.
Winkler shared he thought about becoming a child psychologist before going into acting. (Olivia Wong/WireImage)
'HAPPY DAYS' STAR HENRY WINKLER FILMED HIS FIRST-EVER NUDE SCENE AT 79
The actor has spoken about his lifelong struggle with dyslexia many times in the past and about how he learned to manage it in his career.

"Destiny is very strange, because I've chosen a profession that is so unbelievably difficult, not only to survive in, but to participate in for me," he told "PBS News Weekend" in November 2023. "When we were doing 'Happy Days' or any table read, which is the whole cast all the producers, the directors, everybody on the crew listening, for the first time to the script. I couldn't read off the page. And it was embarrassing. It was humiliating. I covered it with humor."

To manage the obstacles dyslexia presented in his career, Winkler explained that he would "literally read one word at a time" and ask for the script to be delivered to him ahead of time so that he would "almost memorize it" so that by the time it came to the table read, "I could read it with a flow."

While the actor had struggled with dyslexia his whole life, he didn't receive a diagnosis until he was in he was 31, and his young stepson was diagnosed with it, telling PBS that he was initially angry after getting the diagnosis.
Winkler didn't receive a dyslexia diagnosis until he was in his 30s, when his stepson was diagnosed. (MEGA/GC Images)
CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR THE ENTERTAINMENT NEWSLETTER

"I was because I was humiliated. I was constantly browbeaten. I was punished, grounded for most of my life," he said. "Then the next stage was all right, so I have this thing. Now I have to learn to negotiate it because it doesn't go away. It is the wiring in your brain."

He later learned to reframe the situation and began thinking, "maybe I would not be sitting in this chair" if he hadn't gone through "the challenge to constantly work through that made my tenacity, like steel."
Following his time on "Happy Days," Winkler continued acting, introducing himself to a younger audience in the 1998 movie, "The Waterboy," alongside Adam Sandler.

He then appeared in TV shows such as "Arrested Development," "Parks and Recreation" and "New Girl," before landing a starring role in the hit HBO Max show, "Barry," playing Gene Cousineau, an acting coach who finds himself befriending an assassin.

title: Roger Miller given stark choice after getting caught stealing: ‘You can go to jail or you can go in the Army’
summary: Dean Miller says his father joined the Army as a teen after he was caught stealing from a club. The judge then gave him a choice between jail and the Army.
story: Country music star Lee Greenwood discusses the re-launch of his distillery, Soldier Valley Spirits, ahead of America's 250th birthday on 'America Reports.'
Roger Miller's son is getting candid about why his famous father joined the Army as a teenager.

During a recent interview on the "Drifting Cowboy" podcast, the country music legend's son, Dean Miller, discussed how his father grew up "on a farm with no electricity" and would spend the weekends driving to Amarillo, Texas to play shows at a nightclub in an effort to break into the music industry.

"He would play at this one club, and he was friends with the guy and my dad, as he describes it, was ignorant and didn't know how to break into show business or how to get out of town or what to do with his life," he said.

Dean explained that his dad later had the idea that "if he stole a bunch of stuff from this club, he'd have all he needed to be in show business," leading him to steal equipment and costumes. According to the singer's website, he stole a guitar because he wanted it "so desperately to write songs," and turned himself in the next day.
The country singer's son recalled how his father ended up in the Army. (Silver Screen Collection/Hulton Archive/Getty Images)

"The police caught him and the guy that he stole from wrote a letter to the judge and said, 'Please be lenient on this kid. He doesn't know any better. He's a good kid."' And all this stuff," Dean said. "And so they told my dad, 'You can go to jail or you can go in the Army. Your choice.' And he chose the Army."
After joining the Army, Roger was deployed to Korea during the Korean War, which he referred to as the "Korea Clash of '52."
Dean recalled his father telling him that while in Korea, "I just spent the whole time hiding under a jeep and crying."

Ultimately, his time in the Army helped him in his music career, with Dean saying that is where "he met people in music" and was able to get "recommendations to people back home and started coming to Nashville after that."

Roger is often regarded as a major figure in country music, credited for broadening the range of the genre by including elements of pop music in his songs.

Between 1965 and 1966, Roger won 11 Grammy Awards, including best contemporary country album for "Dang Me/Chug-A-Lug," and best country song for "Dang Me" and "King of the Road." He received a total of 18 nominations.

Throughout his career, he also wrote the score for the Broadway musical, "Big River," and the soundtrack for the Disney movie, "Robin Hood." He was inducted into the Country Music Hall of Fame in 1995, three years after his death.

title: Courtney Love reveals secret health crisis that nearly killed her: 'My body just exploded'
summary: Courtney Love shared that her body "just exploded" during a secret health crisis that left her near death. She los all her hair and dropped to 100 pounds.
story: Fox News Flash top entertainment and celebrity headlines are here.
Courtney Love revealed a health battle she kept private for years.

The Hole singer, 62, shared an update about her long-awaited new album, explaining that the record took shape during a period when she was frequently hospitalized and believed it could be her final work.
"I went to England in 2019, and when I went there, you know, my body just exploded," Love said in an Instagram video.
"It just exploded. And I was in hospitals a lot. I almost died. I lost all my hair. I was about 100 pounds. And they told me I was going to die, and I didn’t believe them."
KURT COBAIN AND COURTNEY LOVE ATTEMPTED TO ESCAPE 'CRAZINESS' OF FAME
Courtney Love revealed she was hospitalized repeatedly starting in 2019 and nearly died. (Julien Hekimian/Getty Images)
Love did not identify the illness or illnesses she was battling but said she recovered after refusing to accept the prognosis she had been given.
The singer connected that determination to a memory from childhood, describing a tendency to challenge what adults told her was true.
"When I was a kid — and I think this record is about this — I used to pattern interrupt the adults," she said. "They’d tell me red was blue, and then I’d see blue, but blue was blue.
"So, now that I gaslight myself that maybe they were right, and red was blue, and then I would see purple, and my head would explode. Like f---ing cope with that s---, right?
The Hole singer lost all her hair and dropped to 100 pounds during her private health battle. (Edward Berthelot/Getty Images)

"I never really lost my ability to see that … red was red. Despite them telling me that red was blue. And, so, when they said, 'You’re going to die,’ I just didn’t believe them. And, somehow, I got better. I’m healthy, which is amazing.
"I just wasn’t public about being sick. I don’t want to be public. I’m fine now."
Love wrote her new album while she was ill. (Reuters)
The singer said she wants to return to the road and perform again, describing music as essential to her well-being.
Her new album appears to have emerged directly from the period in which she was fighting to recover.
In an Instagram caption accompanying her video, Love explained that when she began making the record, she believed it might be her last.

Love rose to fame with her band, Hole, and as the wife of Nirvana frontman Kurt Cobain. (Barry King/WireImage)

"I wanted to give you an update on my record. When I made it, I believed this was my last record. So, I made the record I always wanted to make. I was in the hospital mostly but when I wasn’t all I did was write & record it."
Love also thanked those who worked with her while she was dealing with what she described as trauma.
The project would mark a significant return for Love, who has not released an album since Hole’s 2010 "Nobody’s Daughter."

title: Dolly Parton’s ongoing health battle forces country legend to miss major Dollywood event
summary: Dolly Parton appeared virtually at Dollywood's new roller coaster opening after her Nashville doctor grounded her travel over dizziness and dehydration.
story: Dolly Parton says no matter what happens, she’ll always be a country girl at heart.
Country music icon Dolly Parton missed a major Dollywood event Friday after her doctor advised her to stay in Nashville because of continued "health issues."

The 80-year-old "9 to 5" singer was expected to appear in person at the Tennessee theme park for the opening of its new NightFlight Expedition roller coaster, but she joined the celebration virtually after her doctor told her not to travel.
"I’m still in Nashville, and I’m sorry about that," Parton told the crowd during a video appearance at the event, according to video shared by the Knoxville News Sentinel.
DOLLY PARTON'S SISTER OFFERS HEALTH UPDATE ON COUNTRY ICON AFTER FANS WORRY OVER HER CALL FOR PRAYERS
Dolly Parton's ongoing health issues forced her to skip a Dollywood appearance, months after canceling her Las Vegas residency. (Katherine Bomboy/NBC via Getty Images)

"I’m supposed to be there in person, like we planned," she continued. "Now I’ve told you before, all my fans, that I have had a few little health issues. And sometimes I get a little dizzy, and I get dehydrated.
"And I’m dehydrated," Parton, who appeared on-screen wearing fairy wings, told the crowd. "And, so, my Nashville doctor clipped my wings, saying, 'You ain’t traveling this week.’
DOLLY PARTON UNABLE TO WRITE NEW SONGS AFTER LOSING HUSBAND OF NEARLY 60 YEARS
Parton told fans her doctor "clipped my wings" over dehydration and dizziness, keeping her in Nashville. (Jason Kempin/Getty Images)

"So, I guess if your doctor tells you, ‘You ain’t traveling this week,’ you ain’t traveling this week," she continued, explaining she likes keeping her fans "in the loop" and had promised to update them "on everything."

LEANN RIMES CANCELS CONCERTS DUE TO SEVERE ILLNESS, SAYS SHE IS 'TRULY HEARTBROKEN'
Parton’s absence comes as she continues to recover from health problems that have forced her to scale back some of her performance plans.

"It's going to take me a little while before I'm up to stage-performance level, because some of the meds and treatments make me a little bit swimmy-headed, as my grandma used to say," she quipped. "And, of course, I can't be dizzy, carrying around banjos, guitars and such on five-inch heels ... not to mention all those heavy rhinestone outfits, the big hair, my big personality."

title: Actor charged with 24 felony counts in alleged child sexual abuse case
summary: Actor Shane Ryan Gledhill faces 24 felony charges after a nearly five-year investigation alleges he exploited aspiring young actors through casting calls.
story: Fox News Flash top entertainment and celebrity headlines are here.

A California actor and producer is facing 24 felony charges after investigators said he used online casting calls to contact minors as part of an alleged pattern of child sexual abuse spanning decades.
Shane Ryan Gledhill, 46, of Lompoc, was arrested Aug. 3 after Santa Barbara County Sheriff's detectives spent nearly five years investigating accusations of exploitation.
Gledhill, whose work involved projects connected to actors including Shelley Duvall, Tom Arnold, Richard Dreyfuss and Ed Harris, was initially booked on 15 felony charges.
That total has now climbed to 24.
TIMOTHY BUSFIELD INDICTED ON CHILD SEX ABUSE CHARGES IN NEW MEXICO
Shane Ryan Gledhill was arrested Aug. 3. (Santa Barbara Sheriff)

The investigation began in November 2021, when a 17-year-old survivor approached Santa Barbara County Sheriff's investigators about what the alleged victim described as suspicious and inappropriate conduct involving Gledhill when she was 15, according to authorities.
That initial report led to an investigation that eventually identified nine survivors, the sheriff's office said. All were minors at the time of the alleged offenses.
In February 2022, investigators executed a search warrant at his home in Lompoc. Investigators seized thousands of digital files, which underwent an extensive forensic examination.
The sheriff's office said the investigation uncovered a pattern in which Gledhill allegedly used online casting calls and film-making projects to contact aspiring young actors.
LIKE WHAT YOU’RE READING? CLICK HERE FOR MORE ENTERTAINMENT NEWS
Gledhill is being held at the Santa Barbara County jail in California. (Frazer Harrison/Getty Images)
That detail prompted authorities to publicly release his booking photograph.

"The Sheriff’s Office is releasing Gledhill’s booking photograph because detectives believe he often used the professional names ‘Shane Ryan’ and ‘Shane Ryan-Reid’ when contacting aspiring actors and filmmakers.

"Individuals who interacted with him under those names may not recognize his legal name. Detectives hope the photograph will assist in identifying additional survivors or witnesses."
Gledhill faces 24 felony charges. (Frazer Harrison/Getty Images)

The charges against Gledhill include alleged offenses such as child molestation, rape, forcible sexual assault, contacting a minor with the intent to commit a sexual offense, possession of child sexual abuse material and providing harmful matter to a minor.
Gledhill was taken into custody at his Lompoc home on an arrest warrant and booked into the Northern Branch Jail. His bail was set at $2 million.
"Based on evidence developed during the investigation, detectives believe there may be additional survivors who have not yet been identified or come forward," the press release shared.

Investigators believe the alleged conduct could span roughly 25 years, with potential survivors or witnesses located not only along California's Central Coast but also in the Los Angeles area and on the East Coast.

title: ‘A Man Without Love’ singer Engelbert Humperdinck credits underwater workout for keeping him ‘alive’ at 90
summary: Engelbert Humperdinck reveals the underwater pool workout and martial arts routine he credits with keeping him "alive" and performing at age 90.
story: The legendary singer-songwriter discusses his HBO film
At 90, Engelbert Humperdinck has an unusual workout routine he credits with keeping him alive and going strong.
The British singer, known as the "King of Romance," recently appeared on "The Jim Masters Show," where he shared his unconventional exercise regimen.

"I walk out in the pool all the day," he told the host. "I do all my martial art moves in the pool underwater, which makes it even more effective. … And that’s how I stay alive and keep going and keep myself as fit as possible so that the audience can see me in a respectable way.
JOAN COLLINS SHARES HER SIMPLE SECRETS TO AGING GRACEFULLY AT 93
Engelbert Humperdinck performs at Kiri Te Kanawa Theatre June 30, 2026, in Auckland, New Zealand. (Dave Simpson/WireImage)
"That's where I work out there in the pool," he said. "I do all my stuff up there, which is great."
And it appears to be working. The "Release Me" singer is still performing regularly, with concert dates scheduled into 2027 abroad. He's also preparing to release a new album, "Faithfully," Aug. 28.
The album features Humperdinck putting his own spin on songs by Journey, the Cars, Kiss and Aerosmith, with several guest musicians joining him on the record.

While Humperdinck is working to keep his body young, a decades-old song is helping him reach younger audiences. His 1968 track "A Man Without Love" was featured in two episodes of Marvel Studios' "Moon Knight."
Engelbert Humperdinck poses at his home on a Harley-Davidson with a Union flag before traveling to Baku for Eurovision on May 8, 2012, in Leicester, England. (Christopher Furlong/Getty Images)

"Since ‘Man Without Love,’ it’s triggered something off," he said. "And it’s so nice. It’s so nice to know that people are now not worried about an age. They’re worried about the music, and that’s all that counts as far as I’m concerned. But I try to stay as young as possible all the time."

While Humperdinck continues connecting with audiences through the love songs that made him famous, the lyrics have taken on a deeper meaning since his wife, Patricia, died in 2021 after living with Alzheimer's disease and contracting COVID-19. The couple married in 1964 and remained together for 57 years until her death at age 85.

"She’s the backbone. She was the backbone to my whole life, I think, because she started with me when I was nobody. … And so she was instrumental in the early years. And when I really made it in the industry and got a family, I used to have to leave home for about three months at a time. And she raised the children by herself."

Singer Engelbert Humperdinck and wife Patricia Dorsey appear with his star at Paris Las Vegas during his Las Vegas Walk of Stars dedication ceremony July 20, 2011. (Ethan Miller/Getty Images)
While his heartfelt ballads are now bittersweet, Humperdinck still finds joy in performing them for audiences today.

"There's no better feeling. There's no better feeling than walking on stage," he said. "I call myself a thespian of song. So, when I'm singing, I act a part. It's not acting really, it's reality coming through. But I give my all, and I read the lyrics a little differently now, especially since I lost my wife. And it comes out more sincere.

"I’m a ballad singer, and I love, love singing ballads," he said. "There’s nothing like a good romantic ballad to touch the heart. And it puts people together. ... I feel responsible for putting people together."

"And that's just wonderful. That's the kind of legacy I want to leave behind. I want to leave a good taste in my career behind."

story: The ‘Wizards Beyond Waverly Place’ star opens up about his new book, helping kids tackle big fears and using Scripture to build family faith.
Former Disney star David Henrie is opening up about how he rejected the "secular" Hollywood lifestyle after going on a life-changing monastery visit.

Earlier this week, the "Wizards of Waverly Place" star was a guest on Raymond Arroyo's "Arroyo Grande" podcast and discussed how his friendship with fellow actor Kevin James led to him discovering his faith.

"I started changing my whole perspective on life and faith. I so craved an objective belief system. I grew up in relativistic Hollywood and, you know, a partying lifestyle, secular life, worldliness, materialism, and it left me empty," Henrie said.
David Henrie credits a monastery visit in 2012 with changing his life. (Chris Haston/WBTV via Getty Images)

"I call it the bubblegum theory of pleasure. Every time you eat a piece of bubblegum, it loses its flavor. In a few moments, you pop another one in. At the end of the day, you've gone through the whole pack, and now you just feel worse than you did when you started. That was me before I met Kevin," he continued.

Henrie said he found God during this time, and James extended an invitation to him to visit St. Michael's Abbey in Orange County in 2012 and do his general confession.
"And I was like, 'What's that?' So, I learned about what it was, and I wrote a whole chapter book to bring to the priest there," Henrie said.

title: Carmen Electra reveals what she wants in a man after racy Playboy comeback
summary: "Baywatch" star Carmen Electra opens up about dating, confidence and what she truly wants in a partner after her stunning Playboy comeback three decades later.
story: Carmen Electra shares her thoughts on what it takes to keep the ‘spark alive’ in relationships.
After making her Playboy comeback, Carmen Electra says she’s open to hopping back into the dating pool.

At 54, the "Baywatch" bombshell posed for the magazine three decades after her debut. The actress and model first appeared in the magazine in 1996 at age 24 and now graces the pages of its Summer 2026 issue, which is on sale now.
Posing in fishnets, Electra also answered readers' burning questions about love, but she isn't just dishing out dating advice. She's ready for a romance of her own.
MARTHA STEWART GETS CANDID ABOUT PLASTIC SURGERY, DATING AS SHE TURNS 85
Carmen Electra is in the summer 2026 issue of Playboy available now. (Gerome Defrance/Getty Images)

"I still like a guy that's a little bit edgy, but I wouldn't mind being with a dad type," the star told Fox News Digital. "I did actually date a dad. He had a daughter. I fell in love with the daughter. And I kind of thought that was going to be the relationship. Didn't work out, but I could be with someone who has a kid or not."
Carmen Electra plays celebrity bunny dealer at the Playboy Club at The Palms Hotel in Las Vegas Dec. 13, 2008. (Jon Kopaloff/FilmMagic)

The actress and model has walked down the aisle twice before. She wed former NBA star Dennis Rodman in November 1998. Rodman filed for an annulment just nine days later, though the pair reconciled before Electra ultimately filed for divorce in April 1999.
Electra gave marriage another shot with Jane's Addiction guitarist Dave Navarro, saying "I do" in 2003. The couple announced their separation in 2006, and their divorce was finalized in 2007.
CARMEN ELECTRA REVEALS HER SIMPLE RULE FOR KEEPING THE ‘SPARK ALIVE’ IN RELATIONSHIPS
Today, Electra isn't putting any limits on love.

"They don't have to be a dad," she said. "They could be a little bit younger. I don't know. I don't really know who that guy is yet. I work really hard. I make money. I'm not looking for the man with money. That's not my goal.
"If he wants to buy me a few gifts, that's nice. But I can take care of myself. He just has to be a good person. That's very important. And we have to like the same things.

For the summer 2026 issue, Carmen Electra steps in as Playboy advisor and answered pressing questions about love and dating to field readers’ questions about love, confidence and reinvention. (Max Montgomery for Playboy)

"It's also cool when opposites attract," she noted. "Because they say if two people are too similar, one person is unnecessary. So, you don't want it to be too similar, but you do want to like certain things. You want to have some things in common. But you also want to learn from each other."
Electra has long worn her heart on her sleeve and "love" on her skin. The pinup previously told Fox News Digital she has the word tattooed on her wrist.
Carmen Electra has racked up more than 150 covers worldwide. (Max Montgomery for Playboy)

"I've always been about love," Electra said at the time. "I've always come from a place of love. And if we could all do that, what a wonderful place we could be in. If you really mess with me, I don't know how much love you're going to get. But I truly believe in love."
Electra said she has felt plenty of love from her social media followers, who have cheered her on through the years.
Carmen Electra arrives at The Abbey's 35th Anniversary at The Abbey Food & Bar in West Hollywood May 20, 2026. (Steve Granitz/FilmMagic/Getty Images)

"Look, sometimes I'm trying different things on my Instagram page," she said. "Not everyone's going to love those things, and you might not get as many likes. But you turn around and, boom, my fans are there."
CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR THE ENTERTAINMENT NEWSLETTER
Carmen Electra joined "Baywatch" for its eighth season. (Gerome Defrance/Getty Images)

After making a splash in Hollywood, Electra has discovered what makes her feel most confident, and it has nothing to do with looking glamorous or having a beau. For her, it's all about being booked and busy.

"I feel the most confident when I'm working, and I've been working a lot," she said. "When I'm working, I'm really happy. It's weird; you would think that by now I'd be over it. But I'm just not. I love it. And the more I work, the more confident I feel. When I'm in love, I feel confident. But I don't have someone in my life right now. But I'm still confident because I'm working."
Carmen Electra attends the "Scary Movie" global premiere at Paramount Pictures Studios June 3, 2026, in Los Angeles. (Getty Images for Paramount Pictures)
After returning to Playboy, Electra has a message for women who think getting older means fading into the background: Don't buy it.
LIKE WHAT YOU'RE READING? CLICK HERE FOR MORE ENTERTAINMENT NEWS
Carmen Electra is in the new issue of Playboy alongside cover girl Cara Delevingne. (Max Montgomery for Playboy)

"Don't let anyone tell you you're too old," she said. "That's a myth. You are living your own life. You're not living your life for other people. And, honestly, if you're manifesting that, that's what it's going to be for you.

"You have to change your thought process. You have to start telling yourself every morning, 'I'm beautiful. I'm good enough. I look great. I'm pretty.' Whatever it is that you want to be, you can be that.
Carmen Electra arrives at the world premiere of "Infinite Icon: A Visual Memoir" at AMC The Grove 14 in Los Angeles Jan. 20, 2026. (Steve Granitz/FilmMagic)

"At one time in my life, I was reading a lot of books about Buddhism," she reflected. "I remember one book talked about your inner child and never losing your inner child. And I've always been a bit childish.

"So, I always thought, 'I'm not going to lose it.' I never want to lose that, and I'm not going to. And I think the people who are older than me, who are still in this business and who I think are beautiful, have a youthful spirit. And people will love you for being who you really, truly are."
