title: 100 Kodiak driverless trucks are headed for public roads
summary: Atlas Energy Solutions plans to grow its Kodiak driverless truck fleet from 28 to 100 by mid-2027, with public highway driving in Texas and New Mexico.
story: Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson spoke with Daniel Goff, vice president of external affairs at Kodiak AI, about how attitudes toward autonomous trucks have shifted over time.
Atlas Energy Solutions is expanding its fleet of Kodiak-powered driverless trucks across Texas and New Mexico. The trucks already haul sand to oil and gas well sites without anyone inside the cab.

Now, Atlas and Kodiak plan to grow the fleet from 28 driverless trucks to 100 by mid-2027. They also expect the trucks to begin operating on public roads in early 2027. However, that timeline still depends on operational milestones.
The expansion gives us a clearer look at how driverless trucking could move from private industrial roads onto highways.

NEW YORK SCHOOL PAUSES HUMANOID CLASSROOM ROBOT PILOT PROGRAM

Kodiak-powered driverless trucks haul sand across the Permian Basin as Atlas Energy Solutions prepares to expand its autonomous fleet from 28 trucks to 100 by mid-2027. (Photographer: Michael Nagle/Bloomberg via Getty Images)
Kodiak driverless trucks expand to a second depot

Atlas previously operated its driverless trucks from one load-out location at a time. It now runs them simultaneously from two depots about 90 minutes apart. One site is in Texas while the other is in New Mexico. The wider footprint lets Atlas reach more well sites across the Permian Basin. It can also respond faster when customers need more sand delivered. The operation connects with Atlas' 42-mile Dune Express conveyor system. That system moves sand closer to the well sites before the trucks complete the final portion of the trip.

Don Burnette, founder and CEO of Kodiak, said the two companies have built the world's largest fleet of driverless big-rig trucks: "Together, Atlas and Kodiak have deployed the world's largest fleet of driverless big-rig trucks. We've demonstrated that autonomous trucking is delivering meaningful results today. Our expanding partnership, which now covers two unique locations, is creating a blueprint for how autonomy can transform logistics by improving efficiency, increasing productivity, and delivering lasting value for customers at commercial scale."
The driverless fleet is growing from 28 trucks to 100

As of March 31, 2026, Atlas's driverless program operated 28 driverless trucks across 15 routes. Those trucks had carried about 7,000 loads and hauled more than 450,000 tons of sand. The fleet also logged more than 23,500 driverless operating hours during the first quarter of 2026. On July 20, Kodiak-powered trucks delivered 176 loads in one day. The companies called it a daily record for the 18-month deployment.

Earlier in 2026, Kodiak and Atlas also introduced a driverless truck that can pull three connected trailers. The combined loaded weight tops 135 tons. That kind of load would grab anyone's attention. It also raises an obvious question. What happens when these trucks leave private roads and begin driving beside the rest of us?
Public highway driving could begin in 2027

Kodiak plans to launch driverless highway operations by the end of 2026. Atlas expects its Kodiak-equipped fleet to follow onto public highways in 2027. The company is not alone in moving toward humanless highway freight. A separate autonomous truck recently completed a 230-mile commercial delivery in Texas with nobody in the cab.

Burnette told CyberGuy that other motorists should not expect unusual behavior from Kodiak-powered trucks: "Kodiak-powered trucks already operate autonomously on highways across the southern United States with a safety driver in the cab to oversee the system.The Kodiak Driver is engineered to be a safe and cautious driver and to follow normal driving etiquette, so other motorists should not notice anything unusual."

That may sound reassuring. Still, most drivers will want more than a smooth lane change before they feel comfortable beside a truck with no human behind the wheel. CyberGuy recently took a closer look at whether autonomous trucks can make highways safer, including Kodiak's arguments about fatigue, distracted driving and real-world testing.
How driverless trucks handle extreme weather

The Permian Basin can be brutal on vehicles. Trucks can face triple-digit temperatures, dust storms, sudden flooding and high crosswinds. Dense morning fog can also make visibility difficult. Kodiak equips its trucks with a sensor suite built around cameras, with radar and lidar support. These systems give the truck a detailed view of the surrounding environment.

However, more sensors cannot make every condition safe. Burnette said the truck will stop instead of pushing through dangerous weather: "And if conditions aren't safe, the truck won't keep driving. It slows down and safely pulls over." Kodiak says its system responds to construction zones and emergency vehicles as part of normal driving. It also adjusts to changing road conditions. Severe fog or other hazardous weather can still stop an autonomous trip. According to Burnette, Kodiak-powered vehicles will remain parked when conditions become unsafe.
AI KILL SWITCH BILL COULD SHUT DOWN ROGUE MODELS

Atlas Energy Solutions is expanding its fleet of driverless big rigs across Texas and New Mexico, with public highway operations expected to begin in 2027. (Photographer: Michael Nagle/Bloomberg via Getty Images)
What happens when a driverless truck has a problem

A damaged component or communications failure can create a serious problem in any large truck. The stakes may feel even higher when nobody is sitting in the cab. Burnette said the Kodiak Driver checks both the truck and its autonomous system while it operates: "The Kodiak Driver continuously monitors the truck and its autonomous driving system. If it detects a critical problem, such as a mechanical, sensor or communications failure, it can execute a fallback maneuver that safely pulls the truck out of traffic and brings it to a stop in a safe location."
According to Burnette, "The health and safety of all trucks are overseen by Kodiak's command center, and a human can remotely provide assistance should a truck need additional help."
Kodiak points to an independent safety score

Kodiak also cites a safety evaluation from Nauto, an AI-powered fleet safety company. The Kodiak Driver earned a VERA safety score of 98 out of 100. That result tied for the highest score among more than 1,000 commercial fleets in Nauto's network. The other fleets used human drivers. The system earned a perfect score for inattentive driving and high-risk driving. It also earned 100 for traffic violations. Its aggressive driving score was 95. You can read CyberGuy's full breakdown of the Kodiak Driver's independent safety score. Burnette pointed to the evaluation in his response: "We are proud that an independent evaluation by Nauto, a leader in AI-powered fleet safety technology, gave Kodiak the highest score in a safety study, tying for first place and outperforming 1,000 human-driven fleets."
How Kodiak protects driverless trucks from hackers

Driverless trucks create another concern that has nothing to do with rain or road debris. A connected vehicle can become a cybersecurity target. Kodiak does not publicly detail every safeguard. Publishing a complete security blueprint could help attackers. Burnette said Kodiak treats cybersecurity as part of its safety work: "Cybersecurity is something we take extremely seriously because safety starts long before a truck ever reaches the road."

He said Kodiak uses multiple security layers and continuously watches for suspicious activity. The company also tightly limits access to its systems. "We build multiple layers of security into our vehicles and systems to help protect against unauthorized access, and we continuously monitor for unusual activity. For security reasons, we don't discuss the specific safeguards we use or how they're implemented. But access to the systems is tightly controlled and if it detects something unusual, it will bring itself to a safe stop rather than continuing to operate." Kodiak's public technology materials say the company isolates safety-critical functions from external communication ports. It also says it protects vehicle infrastructure with end-to-end encryption.
What this means to you

You probably will not wake up tomorrow and find every delivery truck driving itself. Early public deployments will likely focus on routes where operators already understand the conditions. Still, the Atlas expansion shows that fully driverless trucking has entered commercial service. These trucks are already working without a person in the cab.

The next major step will bring them onto roads used by commuters and families. Other truck drivers will also begin sharing lanes with autonomous rigs. For you, the biggest issue is how the system responds when normal driving suddenly becomes abnormal. Dangerous weather can change a trip in seconds. So can equipment failures, cyberattacks or unpredictable motorists.

Kodiak says its system will reduce speed and move toward a safe stop when conditions become unsafe. Human teams will also monitor the fleet through a command center. The technology could eventually affect deliveries and transportation costs. It may also change trucking jobs, an issue CyberGuy explored in a closer look at whether autonomous trucks could replace drivers by 2027.

As these vehicles reach public highways, transparency will become even more important. Drivers deserve clear information about crash reporting and emergency response. They also need to understand the limits of remote assistance. Regulators will need to test company safety claims against real-world results. A strong safety score provides a starting point, but public trust will depend on consistent performance over time.
OUR ENEMIES FOUND A WEAKNESS IN ESSENTIAL TECHNOLOGY. WE MUST FIX IT … FAST

Kodiak-powered trucks already move heavy loads without anyone in the cab, logging more than 23,500 driverless operating hours in the first quarter of 2026. (Photographer: Michael Nagle/Bloomberg via Getty Images)
Kurt's key takeaways

Kodiak and Atlas are rapidly expanding a commercial driverless truck operation that already moves heavy loads without anyone in the cab. The plan to grow from 28 trucks to 100 by mid-2027 shows how quickly autonomous trucking can scale inside a demanding industrial environment. Public highway use will bring a new level of scrutiny. Drivers will want answers about severe weather, system failures, public-road emergencies and cybersecurity. Kodiak says its trucks can stop when something goes wrong. Human teams also remain available through a command center. However, the technology must prove that those protections work reliably as more trucks enter service. The expansion could reshape how companies transport essential materials. Yet public trust will depend on what happens when these trucks encounter the unpredictable moments every driver knows too well.
Would you feel comfortable driving beside a 135-ton truck with no one in the cab if the company said its AI could handle the unexpected? Let us know by writing to us at CyberGuy.com.

title: Brinks Home data breach puts 1M customers on alert
summary: Brinks Home confirmed unauthorized access to its IT systems, and the ShinyHunters group claims it stole 4.9 million Salesforce records from it.
story: Cybersecurity expert Theresa Payton breaks down age verification, AI tools and how to protect kids online without collecting biometric or personal data that can be hacked.

You hire a home security company to help protect your house. So, hearing that hackers broke into the company's own computer systems may feel especially unsettling. Brinks Home has confirmed that an unauthorized party accessed part of its IT environment. The Dallas-based company says its alarm monitoring and security systems continue to work normally.

However, the intruder has threatened to release information it claims to have stolen. The Brinks Home data breach could affect a wide audience. Brinks Home says it serves residential customers in all 50 states. It also says it protects more than 1 million people across North America. For now, customers face a frustrating gap. Brinks Home has not confirmed exactly what information was accessed or who may be affected.
New! Free live CyberGuy class: Protect Your Money From Today’s Biggest Threats

Join us Saturday, Aug. 29, at 10 a.m. ET for a free CyberGuy LIVE class covering five simple steps to help defend yourself against AI scams, fraud, identity theft and financial hacks. Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson will explain how to set up bank alerts, strengthen your account logins, protect your phone number, freeze your credit and help secure your retirement savings against unauthorized transfers. No technical experience is needed. You’ll also receive our financial protection checklist, and every registrant will get a link to the class recording afterward.
Reserve your free spot today at CyberGuyLive.com.
COULD THE 7-ELEVEN BREACH AFFECT YOU?

Brinks Home confirmed an unauthorized party accessed part of its IT environment, though the company says its alarm monitoring and security systems continue to operate normally. (Photographer: Shelby Tauber/Bloomberg via Getty Images)
What Brinks Home confirmed about the cyberattack

Brinks Home discovered unauthorized access to part of its systems on July 20, 2026. The company activated its incident response procedures and moved to contain the intrusion. It also brought in outside cybersecurity experts to investigate. William Niles, CEO of Brinks Home, said the company was working with leading forensic experts to address the incident.

CyberGuy reached out to Brinks Home for additional comment. The company confirmed that its response began as soon as it detected the intrusion. "Brinks Home recently identified a security incident in which an unauthorized party gained access to certain company systems. Upon discovering the incident, we immediately activated our incident response plan, contained the activity, and engaged an industry-leading cybersecurity forensics firm to investigate," Brinks Home told CyberGuy.

The company's most reassuring update involves its security services. Brinks Home says the incident did not involve its products or monitoring services based on what it knows so far. Your security panel and sensors should continue working. Emergency monitoring should also remain available without interruption. However, the investigation has not determined the full scope of the incident.

Brinks Home stressed that its investigation remains in the early stages. "Our investigation is early and ongoing. Our systems are secure, and we are continuing to assess the full scope and potential impact of the incident while closely monitoring our environment," the company said. "If we determine that your information was affected, we will notify you and explain what steps, if any, you should take," the company says in its cybersecurity FAQ.
Hackers claim they stole 4.9 million Brinks Home records

The ShinyHunters extortion group has claimed responsibility for the attack. The gang alleges that it stole more than 4.9 million records from Brinks Home's Salesforce environment. That number refers to database records. It does not mean 4.9 million separate people were affected. One customer may appear in several records.

According to ShinyHunters, the stolen information includes more than 1.1 million rows from a Salesforce customer contacts database. The hackers also claim they obtained more than 4,000 employee records. Those records allegedly contain names, email addresses, job titles and phone numbers. In addition, the group claims it stole around 3.8 million customer support chat logs from the Brinks Care Cresta platform. Those claims have not been independently verified.

BleepingComputer says it has not reviewed the allegedly stolen data. The publication could not confirm the hackers' figures or descriptions. Brinks Home has not confirmed that those specific records were taken. It also has not confirmed that personal information was compromised. That distinction is important. Criminal groups often mix real information with inflated claims to increase pressure on a company. The FBI has warned that ShinyHunters uses real or exaggerated claims while demanding payment. The gang may also use threatening messages or harassing phone calls.
A voice phishing call may have opened the door

ShinyHunters told BleepingComputer that it entered Brinks Home's systems on July 13. The group claims it used a Microsoft Entra voice phishing attack. This type of attack is also called vishing. During a vishing attack, a criminal calls an employee while pretending to work for the company's technology department.

The caller may say the employee needs to complete an account update. The criminal then guides the employee through an authentication or device registration process. If the employee approves the request, the hacker may gain access to the account and its connected business tools. Brinks Home has not confirmed this version of events. Its FAQ says the company is still investigating the incident.

Still, the allegation highlights a growing problem. A hacker may not need to crack a password when an employee can be persuaded to approve access. Voice phishing has helped criminals break into other corporate cloud accounts. That makes unexpected login requests especially dangerous.
Why stolen customer support chats could fuel convincing scams

A customer support chat may sound less sensitive than a password. However, those conversations can contain useful personal details. You may have discussed an installation date or a billing problem. Perhaps you mentioned the equipment installed in your house. A chat could also reveal your contact details, previous service issues or the names of authorized account users. Criminals can use those details to make a scam feel familiar.

For example, a caller might know that you recently contacted Brinks Home. The person could mention your equipment before claiming that an urgent security update is required. That context may make the call sound legitimate. It can also lower your guard before the criminal asks for a password or authentication code. The FBI warns that criminals can use stolen real-world context to create highly convincing phishing campaigns. You can learn more about how exposed contact information helps criminals launch attacks in our guide to ways scammers can use your phone number.
Brinks Home warns customers about follow-up scams

Brinks Home is warning customers to stay alert for suspicious communications related to the breach. A scammer might pretend to represent Brinks Home. The person could also claim to be a cybersecurity investigator or another party involved in the response. The message may say that your data will be released unless you act immediately. It could direct you to a fake login page or ask you to confirm account credentials.

Brinks Home says it will never ask you to provide sensitive information through an unsolicited communication. That warning deserves your attention even though the company has not confirmed whose data was involved. Hackers do not need a complete customer database to start sending scams. They may use public information or previously stolen data to target people while news of the breach spreads.
Has the alleged Brinks Home data been released?

ShinyHunters threatened to release the alleged data if Brinks Home did not respond by July 30, 2026. That deadline has passed. However, as of today, Brinks Home had not publicly confirmed that customer information had been released. Its official update continued to say that the company was investigating what information may have been involved.

The absence of a confirmed leak does not prove that the hackers lack the information. At the same time, the group's claims should not be treated as established facts without evidence. Customers should focus on what they can control now. That includes securing their accounts and becoming more suspicious of unexpected requests.
Tips to stay safe after the Brinks Home data breach
These steps can help protect your accounts, devices and identity while Brinks Home continues its investigation.

Be cautious if someone contacts you about the breach and asks you to confirm personal information. A scammer may claim that your alarm will stop working. The person might also say your account needs an urgent security update. Do not use a link or phone number included in the message. Instead, open the official Brinks Home app yourself. You can also type the company's website address directly into your browser.

Do not trust a caller simply because the person knows your name or account details. Hang up and contact Brinks Home through the app or its official website. Avoid calling a number supplied by the person who contacted you. The FBI recommends verifying unusual requests through a separate communication method before responding.

A legitimate representative should not ask you to read aloud a one-time security code. That code may be the final step a criminal needs to enter your account. End the call if someone asks for one. Also, never approve an unexpected login notification. Select deny or reject when you did not initiate the request.

Change your password if you reused it on another website. You should also change it if you notice unusual account activity or receive an unfamiliar login alert. Create a long password that you have never used for another account. A password manager can create and store a different password for every login. That way, one exposed password cannot unlock several accounts. Pay close attention to your email password. Your email account may control password resets for Brinks Home and many other services.
FAKE SHINYHUNTERS SEXTORTION EMAIL USES CARNIVAL BREACH DATA

Hackers linked to the ShinyHunters extortion group say they stole millions of records from Brinks Home, but the company has not verified those claims. (Photographer: Shelby Tauber/Bloomberg via Getty Images)

A data removal service can request that data brokers and people-search websites remove your personal information. This may include your home address, phone number and relatives' names. Removing those details can make it harder for scammers to combine breached records with information found elsewhere online. However, a data removal service cannot erase information already taken from Brinks Home. It also cannot guarantee that stolen data will disappear from criminal forums. Its value comes from reducing the extra information scammers can use to build a convincing profile about you. Data broker profiles can reappear, so ongoing monitoring and repeated removal requests may be necessary. Check out my top picks for data removal services and get a free scan to find out if your personal information is already out on the web by visiting CyberGuy.com.

Multifactor authentication adds another check after you enter your password. An authenticator app or physical security key can offer stronger protection than a code sent through a text message. Turn on the strongest option available for your Brinks Home account. You should also protect your primary email account. Our guide to the top multifactor authentication apps explains how these tools work.

Open the Brinks Home app or customer portal and review your account information. Check your email address and phone number. Look for unfamiliar authorized users or account changes. Confirm that your emergency contacts and recovery information remain correct. If you ever shared an alarm code or verbal security password in a support chat, contact Brinks Home through an official channel. Ask whether that credential should be changed. Do not change settings through a link sent in an unexpected message.

An exposed phone number can help a criminal attempt a SIM swap or number transfer scam. Contact your wireless carrier and add an account PIN. Ask whether it offers a port-out lock or number transfer lock. These protections can make it harder for someone to transfer your phone number and intercept security codes. You should also use an authenticator app instead of text-message codes when an account offers that choice.

Install strong antivirus software on your computer and mobile devices. This protection can help detect malicious links, fake websites and suspicious downloads before they cause harm. It may also warn you when a phishing page tries to steal your password. Antivirus software cannot reverse the Brinks Home breach. However, it can provide another layer of defense against scams that follow it. Keep the antivirus software updated and allow it to run automatic scans. You should also install operating system, browser and app updates as they become available. Strong antivirus tools can block malware, dangerous websites and unsafe downloads in real time. Get my picks for the best 2026 antivirus protection winners for your Windows, Mac, Android & iOS devices at Cyberguy.com

Brinks Home has not confirmed that Social Security numbers or financial account details were involved. Therefore, customers do not currently have evidence that they all need to replace payment cards. Still, review your bank statements and credit card activity. Watch for small charges that you do not recognize. Check your credit reports for new accounts or unfamiliar inquiries. Our guide to quiet signs of identity theft explains what can appear before larger problems surface. You may also consider an identity theft monitoring service if Brinks Home later confirms that sensitive personal information was exposed.

A credit freeze can make it harder for a criminal to open a new account in your name. You must place the freeze separately with Equifax, Experian and TransUnion. Adding or removing a freeze is free. However, a credit freeze cannot stop misuse of an existing bank or credit card account. Brinks Home has not confirmed that customers need to freeze their credit because of this incident. That recommendation could change if the company identifies exposed identity information.

Brinks Home tells customers not to respond to a suspicious message or click its links. However, the company also says not to delete the communication right away. Take screenshots and preserve the sender's details. Save the date, time and phone number or email address involved. Then report the message using the contact information listed in the official Brinks Home incident FAQ. The company lists 469-391-4024 as a reporting number. You can also report online fraud or extortion attempts to the FBI's Internet Crime Complaint Center at IC3.

Brinks Home says it will contact affected individuals if its investigation confirms that personally identifiable information was involved. However, criminals may send fake breach notices first. Compare any notice with information posted on the official Brinks Home cybersecurity update at brinkshome.com/cybersecurity-update. Contact the company directly when something looks unusual. Do not pay anyone who threatens to release your information.

Brinks Home says it plans to provide more information once its investigation produces verified findings. "Protecting the information entrusted to Brinks Home remains a top priority, and we take our data security responsibilities very seriously. We appreciate the patience and understanding of our customers as we work through this process. We will provide additional updates as appropriate when more verified information becomes available," the company told CyberGuy.

While Brinks Home serves more than 1 million customers nationwide, its recent cybersecurity incident shows that even a company trusted to protect homes can face digital vulnerabilities, despite assurances that alarm monitoring and system functionality continue without interruption. There are many other options in the market, whether you prefer a professionally installed system or a do-it-yourself one.

For reference, you can check out my guide on the best home security systems at Cyberguy.com, where I’ve listed four of my favorite options. You might also want to find out if your home insurance offers a discount for installing robust security protection.
IS YOUR SOCIAL SECURITY NUMBER ON THE DARK WEB?

Brinks Home says it discovered unauthorized access to certain company systems July 20 and brought in outside cybersecurity experts to investigate. (Photographer: Shelby Tauber/Bloomberg via Getty Images)
Kurt's key takeaways

The Brinks Home cyberattack feels personal because this company may hold information connected to your household. So far, Brinks Home has confirmed unauthorized access to part of its IT environment. It has not verified the hackers' claim that they stole 4.9 million Salesforce records. The company says its alarm monitoring and security products continue to work normally. Customers do not need to disconnect their systems based on the information available now. The immediate danger may come from phishing. A criminal who knows your name or previous support issue can build a message that sounds convincing. Slow down when someone creates urgency. Contact Brinks Home through an official channel and never hand over a security code.
When a company is trusted to help protect your home, should it face a higher standard for guarding the personal information connected to it? Let us know by writing to us at CyberGuy.com.

title: Apple Pay text scam threatens $8,250 loss in 35 minutes
summary: Paul C. in Washington, D.C., received an Apple Pay scam text claiming $8,250 was charged and a duplicate would auto-approve within 35 minutes.
story: JPMorgan Chase Head of Consumer Fraud and Scam Prevention Darius Kingsley discusses bank scams in an interview with Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson for the "Beyond Connected" podcast.

Paul C. in Washington, D.C., received an alarming text claiming Apple Pay had already charged him $8,250 and another $8,250 would go through in 35 minutes. That is the kind of message designed to make your stomach drop before you have time to think.
Paul did the smart thing. He stopped, avoided the callback number and sent the text to us. Let's break down every red flag and show you how to verify a charge without handing control to a scammer.
New! Free live CyberGuy class: Protect Your Money From Today’s Biggest Threats

Join us Saturday, Aug. 29, at 10 a.m. ET for a free CyberGuy LIVE class covering five simple steps to help defend yourself against AI scams, fraud, identity theft and financial hacks. Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson will explain how to set up bank alerts, strengthen your account logins, protect your phone number, freeze your credit and help secure your retirement savings against unauthorized transfers. No technical experience is needed. You’ll also receive our financial protection checklist, and every registrant will get a link to the class recording afterward.
Reserve your free spot today at CyberGuyLive.com.
FAKE BOOKING.COM TRAVEL CREDIT SCAM TARGETS TRAVELERS
A scam text falsely warns of an $8,250 Apple Pay charge and threatens another $8,250 transaction within 35 minutes to pressure recipients into calling scammers. (Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson)
The Apple Pay scam text Paul received

The message claimed $8,250 had already been charged through Apple Pay and warned that a duplicate $8,250 transaction would "auto-approve" in 35 minutes. It told Paul to call an 855 number, quote "Case CA-3321" and "verbally kill the pending charge." We partially masked the callback number so no one calls it accidentally.
Every red flag hiding in this Apple Pay scam text
The message looks chaotic, but nearly every phrase has a purpose. The sender uses dramatic wording, fake authority and a tight deadline to push Paul toward one action: calling the number in the text.

The message came from a number beginning with +44, the international calling code for the United Kingdom. Yet it claims to come from "Apple Pay Account Services" and tells Paul in Washington, D.C., to call a separate 855 toll-free number. A different callback number does not automatically prove fraud. However, an overseas sender directing a U.S. recipient to an unrelated support line should make you stop before calling.

The text uses the Apple Pay name several times and signs off as "Apple Pay Account Services." It also arrived as a blue iMessage with the word "Encrypted" shown beneath it. Those details can make the message feel official. However, encryption only means the message was protected while traveling between devices. It does not confirm that Apple sent it. The signature also sounds generic. It does not name Paul's bank, identify the card involved or provide an official Apple support channel.

The first line reads: "$8,250.00 APPLE PAY - 35-MINUTE DEADLINE." The message then claims $8,250 has already disappeared and warns that a duplicate $8,250 charge will be approved in 35 minutes. That raises the threatened loss to $16,500. The exact 35-minute deadline feels calculated. It gives Paul enough time to call while discouraging him from checking Wallet, opening his bank's app or asking someone else for advice.

The message says Paul's Apple Pay account has "hemorrhaged" money. It calls the situation a "catastrophic fraud event" and claims his contactless limit has been "crushed" to $0. It later tells him to "verbally kill the pending charge." Those words sound dramatic because they are meant to produce fear. A legitimate financial alert would normally use clear terms such as charged, declined, frozen or pending. It would not describe an account as hemorrhaging money or ask you to kill a charge.

The first transaction allegedly happened at: "an agricultural processing surplus in Stockton, CA." The second supposedly involved: "a payday lending chain in Modesto." Neither phrase identifies an actual merchant. They sound specific at first because they include industries and real California cities. However, they fall apart when you look closer. A legitimate transaction alert would usually show the merchant's name. It would not rely on vague descriptions such as "agricultural processing surplus."

The sender claims Paul's contactless spending limit has been "crushed to $0." In the same message, it says the second $8,250 transaction is pending and "will auto-approve in 35 minutes." Those claims do not fit together. If the sender had already blocked contactless activity, why would another contactless charge automatically go through? The contradiction matters because it shows the message was written to create panic rather than explain a real account problem.

The message says: "Do not ignore this." It then orders Paul: "You must call." The sender provides a case number, tells him to "verbally kill" the charge and warns that the money will be "gone forever" if he fails to respond. It also threatens to blacklist his account and calls this his "only warning." That language gives Paul one supposed solution: call the number in the text. The message never tells him to open Wallet, check his bank's official app or call the number printed on his card. That is the biggest red flag of all. Every part of the message funnels him toward a stranger waiting on the other end of the phone.
AMAZON RECALL TEXT SCAM COMES WITH RED FLAGS

Apple Pay users should verify suspicious charges through Wallet, their bank’s official app or the number printed on their card — not contact information in an unexpected text. (Qilai Shen/Bloomberg via Getty Images)
How this Apple Pay callback scam likely works

The text serves as bait. The phone call allows the scammer to take control of the conversation. Once you call, the person may claim to see your account. They could ask for your name, card number or Apple Account email. Next, they may request a verification code and describe it as a way to cancel the charge.

A scammer could also ask you to install a remote-access app. That would let the person view your screen or guide you through financial transactions. Some callback scams eventually instruct people to transfer money into a "safe" account. Others claim they sent an oversized refund and demand that the extra money be returned.

The FTC warns that fake support agents may seek remote access, steal card information or convince people to move money. CyberGuy previously heard from another person whose Apple Pay scam text nearly led to a $15,000 loss. In that case, the caller used personal information and pressure to keep her on the phone while she drove to her bank.
Do not call the number in the text. Instead, check through channels you already trust:

Open the Wallet app on your iPhone.Select the credit or debit card involved.Tap the Transactions tab.Review the latest activity.Open your bank or card issuer's official app for the full account history.Call the number on the back of the physical card if anything looks wrong.
Open the Wallet app on your iPhone.
Select the credit or debit card involved.
Tap the Transactions tab.
Review the latest activity.
Open your bank or card issuer's official app for the full account history.
Call the number on the back of the physical card if anything looks wrong.

Apple notes that Wallet may not display the complete transaction history for every card. Your bank or card issuer remains the best source for questions about an Apple Pay charge. Do not rely on a phone number from a text, caller ID or sponsored search result.
How to report the fake Apple Pay text
Before deleting the message, save a screenshot that includes the sender information.
On an iPhone:

Tap Report Spam or Report Junk under the message, depending on what appears.Block the sender.Delete the conversation.Email the screenshot to reportphishing@apple.com.Forward the unwanted text to 7726, which spells SPAM.File a report with the FTC at ReportFraud.ftc.gov.
Tap Report Spam or Report Junk under the message, depending on what appears.
Block the sender.
Delete the conversation.

title: Virginia State University shooting suspect found hiding in dorm closet arrested
summary: Camron Harris was found hiding in a campus dorm closet after an hours-long manhunt following the Virginia State University shooting that wounded five.
story: At least five people were shot outside Virginia State University residence halls, campus officials say.
Virginia police arrested a 19-year-old suspect in connection with a mass shooting at Virginia State University on Saturday.
Authorities named Camron Harris of Henrico, Virginia, noting that he is not a student at the university. The Saturday shooting left five people wounded, one of whom was in critical condition.
Police have not identified any of the victims, but said only one of them is a university student.
There was an hours-long manhunt following the shooting, and police say they ultimately found Harris hiding in a closet inside one of the campus dorm buildings.
POLICE ANNOUNCE ARREST AFTER 5 WOUNDED IN VIRGINIA STATE UNIVERSITY SHOOTING: REPORT
This Nov. 12, 2023 file photo shows the campus of Virginia State University. (USA TODAY Network via Reuters Connect)
Police obtained felony warrants for four counts of malicious wounding and four counts of use of a firearm in the commission of a felony.
Harris is being held without bail at Chesterfield County Jail, according to authorities. They say he may face more charges.
The shooting itself took place early Saturday morning, while Harris was arrested hours later.
MANHUNT UNDERWAY AFTER COLLEGE STUDENT FATALLY SHOT CHASING ROBBERS WHO ALLEGEDLY STOLE HIS PHONE
Chesterfield Police arrested 19-year-old Camron Harris in connection with a mass shooting at Virginia State University on Saturday, August 15. (WWBT via AP; Chesterfield County Police Department)

"Officers responded to the 3300 block of Boisseau Street at approximately 1:28 a.m. and discovered five individuals suffering from gunshot wounds outside VSU residence halls," a university official told Fox News Digital.

"We recognize the concern this incident has caused among our students, parents, alumni, friends and the broader VSU community," the university said in a statement Saturday afternoon. "VSU police will maintain an increased presence on campus as the investigation continues.
"Students should monitor their VSU email for additional safety measures currently in effect and information about available support resources," the statement added.

title: Florida man on probation allegedly kills and dismembers stepfather, stuffs body parts in suitcases
summary: Security footage and three suitcases led Orlando investigators to charge Jose Proano with the murder and dismemberment of his 71-year-old stepfather.
story: Jose Proano, 44, was arrested by the Orange County Sheriff's Office after his blood was found and cell tower data showed his phone "pinging" at the scene of the crime. (Orange County Sheriff's Office)
A Florida man who was on probation has been charged with first-degree murder after allegedly stalking, murdering and dismembering his 71-year-old stepfather.
What led authorities to suspect Jose Proano was a grisly discovery in three suitcases just before midnight on Aug. 4.
The pieces of luggage were found along a roadway in Orlando near the home of Proano’s mother and stepfather.
FLORIDA MAN ARRESTED AFTER SUSPECTED HUMAN REMAINS FOUND BURIED AT PROPERTY WHERE HIS FATHER LIVED
Jose Proano, 44, faces a first-degree murder charge after allegedly killing and dismembering his stepfather. (Orange County Corrections)
About 23 hours earlier, the family of Jorge Vazquez-Escutia called for help.
They’d found his phone, wallet and keys at his home and what looked like blood on the fence outside, according to an affidavit filed in Florida’s Ninth Judicial Circuit Court.

His cars were in his driveway with the doors unlocked, which was unusual, a family member told authorities. They hadn’t seen him in three days, they told deputies with the Orange County Sheriff’s Office.
And friends of his stepson had reached out to the family with a shocking claim – that Jose Proano had told them he’d killed his stepfather, court records show.
The sheriff’s office quickly took to social media asking for the public’s help finding Vazquez-Escutia because of "concerns for Jorge's wellbeing, as he suffers from memory loss."
Then footage from a neighbor’s security camera showed a disturbing series of events.
On the morning of Aug. 2, the day after the missing man was last seen, the security video showed a man wearing a black shirt jumping over the back wall of Vazquez-Escutia’s home.
Jorge Vazquez-Escutia was reported missing by his family in early August before pieces of his body were found in luggage near his home. (Orange County Sheriff's Office)
Later, the same man appears at the back of the house "bringing out suitcases … and ultimately placing what appeared to be a human arm, into the suitcase," court records show.
WISCONSIN TEEN SENTENCED TO LIFE IN BRUTAL SLAYING OF 5-YEAR-OLD BOY FOUND IN DUMPSTER
And at about 4:28 p.m., the video shows the man in black walking down the driveway, carrying three pieces of luggage.
The suitcases "appeared heavy, as the male's left tricep muscle was clearly flexed as he was pulling them," detectives reported.
Investigators called Proano, 44, and asked to meet with them. They’d reviewed his phone records, which showed it had been in the area about the same time the man in black was seen on security video.
Slowly, they pieced together a timeline.
Jorge Vazquez-Escutia's remains were found in the Orlando area. (iStock)
Days earlier, Proano traveled to the area from Northport, about 150 miles away. Proano’s ex-wife told authorities he’d been "acting erratic, making threats towards her," court records show.
ARIZONA MAN ACCUSED OF KILLING WOMAN AFTER SOCIAL MEDIA FIRST DATE ENDS IN DESERT GRAVE
Proano agreed to meet with investigators, court records show.

He told them he had a "negative relationship" with his stepfather, and believed Vazquez-Escutia had "restricted his ability to see his mother." He also told investigators about his schizophrenia, which causes voices in his head that lead "him to worry about members of his family."

Records showed he’d made numerous calls to 911 asking for someone to check on his mother. He believed "bad things were happening," records with the Orange County Sheriff’s Office show. Deputies checked, found all was well at the home, and reported back to reassure him, records show.

Just before midnight on Aug. 4, deputies searched the area surrounding Vazquez-Escutia’s home. They suspected the three suitcases could hold important clues.

Then they happened upon one with an ominous odor lying behind a nearby brick wall. And when a crime scene investigator flipped it open, she found a human head. It belonged to Vazquez-Escutia, records show.

Two more pieces of luggage were found about 400 feet away along a roadway. Dangling from them were luggage tags with Proano’s mother’s name.

Unzipping them and flipping them open, the technician found tarps and more body parts of the missing man.

title: Serial killer survivor who escaped 18-hour captivity reveals instinct she wishes she never ignored
summary: Kara Robinson Chamberlain ignored a split-second intuition before Richard Evonitz abducted her at 15. Now she hosts "Somebody Knows Something."
story: The two-part special, ‘The Amazon Review Killer,’ is now streaming on Fox Nation.
This story discusses suicide. If you or someone you know is having thoughts of suicide, please contact the Suicide & Crisis Lifeline at 988 or 1-800-273-TALK (8255).
Kara Robinson Chamberlain was just 15 years old when she was abducted by a serial killer. Now, she's searching for answers in cases that have gone unsolved for decades.

The victim advocate hosts the ABC News Studios and Freeform true-crime series "Somebody Knows Something," which takes a fresh look at unsolved disappearances and murders that have baffled investigators. Working alongside loved ones, Chamberlain revisits a cold case in each episode, hoping renewed attention will generate the lead that finally cracks it.
SLAIN DAD'S DAUGHTER KNEW ‘BLACK SWAN’ EX-BALLERINA SHOT HIM AFTER ONE CALL: 'SHE KILLED HIM, DIDN'T SHE?'

Kara Robinson Chamberlain, who survived being abducted by serial killer Richard Evonitz, is the host of the new true-crime series Somebody Knows Something, which investigates cold cases. (ABC News Studios/Freeform)

"My purpose was to let families have the mic and show what law enforcement has done," Chamberlain told Fox News Digital. "We want people to have the information they need, so they can come forward with anything that could be helpful. Several of these cases involve children, young people. I have three kids, so I found myself identifying with either the young person who is missing or the victims themselves as parents.
"I genuinely think we can make a difference," Chamberlain said. "If I can get answers for one of these families, it would be a life goal for me."
That mission is deeply personal for Chamberlain, whose own story of survival began more than two decades ago.
Kara Robinson Chamberlain was abducted by serial killer Richard Evonitz from her friend's yard in 2002. (Kara Robinson Chamberlain)
On June 24, 2002, 15-year-old Chamberlain was at a friend's home in South Carolina when Richard Evonitz, the man who would abduct her, pulled into the driveway.

"There was a moment when my captor pulled into my friend's driveway, and I thought, 'That's weird,'" she recalled. "That was my intuition. But I immediately started making excuses for why he could have been there, what could have been the reason. And so, I quieted my intuition."
It was a split-second instinct Chamberlain would soon wish she had trusted.
FOLLOW THE FOX TRUE CRIME TEAM ON X
Kara Robinson Chamberlain was able to escape captivity in Richard Evonitz's Columbia, South Carolina, apartment in 2002. (Kara Robinson Chamberlain)

The stranger approached her with pamphlets and asked if her parents were home. Then, he held a gun to her neck and threatened to shoot her if she screamed. He forced Chamberlain into a dark storage container in his car.

"I'm often asked, 'What's the thing that we can learn from your story, Kara, to keep ourselves or our children safe?'" she said. "And the one thing that I tell people the most is there's a great book called 'The Gift of Fear.' And it's the first time that I've heard someone describe the way I feel, which is to listen to your intuition."

After escaping, Kara Robinson Chamberlain went straight to law enforcement. She provided crucial information that led investigators to her captor’s apartment and helped identify him as the man responsible for at least three previously unsolved murders. (FOX Image Collection via Getty Images)

"Essentially, what the 'Gift of Fear' describes is that we all have something inside of us that's paying attention, and we're taught to silence that intuition for the sake of being nice, not hurting someone's feelings — lots of different reasons. And that's something that is meant to keep us alive."

"I hesitate to say if there's a lesson in these cases because they're all quite different," she continued. "But that's the big thing that I try to tell people — listen to your intuition and teach your children how to listen to that intuition. It is a powerful gift that everyone has, and it saves your life."
In "Somebody Knows Something," Kara Robinson Chamberlain speaks to loved ones and investigators. (ABC News Studios/Freeform)
At Evonitz's apartment, Chamberlain was repeatedly sexually assaulted. But this time, she trusted the instinct telling her what to do: survive.
"I have to acknowledge that there was something inside of me that said, 'Not today. Not me. I'm going to outsmart this guy,'" Chamberlain said, describing herself as "very stubborn."

"Then, I think really the rest of it was maybe part luck," she said. "It was also a big part of my coping mechanism ... how I chose to appease my captor, which essentially is one of the lesser-known trauma responses. It's basically playing nice to let that person put their guard down. And then, I think partially, there's this part of him that was very arrogant, and he'd done that multiple times before. So I think all of those things played together in terms of my escape."
SIGN UP TO GET THE TRUE CRIME NEWSLETTER
Kara Robinson Chamberlain previously appeared in "America's Most Wanted" opposite John Walsh to raise awareness about the stories of victims. (FOX Image Collection via Getty Images)
For 18 hours, Chamberlain was held captive. Throughout the ordeal, she quietly memorized as many details as she could about her surroundings.
Once her captor fell asleep, she managed to free herself from her bindings and escaped. Chamberlain found people sitting in a car in a parking lot and pleaded with them to take her to police.

"Anyone who learns my story ... tends to be sometimes confused by how I tell my story, which is very direct, very to the point, kind of unemotional," she explained. "And that's because my trauma response was to dissociate. ... That enabled me to get through."
Deceased serial killer Richard Evonitz was linked to the killings of three teenage girls between 1996 and 1997. (FBI)

After arriving at a police station, Chamberlain led officers back to her captor's apartment. But when investigators arrived, Evonitz had escaped. Investigators learned Evonitz had taken Chamberlain to the apartment he shared with his wife, who was away at Walt Disney World, according to The Washington Post.
Police tracked Evonitz to Sarasota, Florida. As police closed in on him, Evonitz died by suicide. He was 38.

Evidence recovered from Evonitz’s apartment, former residences and vehicle linked him to the abductions and murders of three girls from Spotsylvania County, Virginia — Sofia Silva, 16; Kristin Lisk, 15; and her sister, Kati Lisk, 12. Notes discovered by investigators indicated that Evonitz already had his eye on other potential victims, Fox News Digital previously reported.
GET REAL-TIME UPDATES DIRECTLY ON THE TRUE CRIME HUB

Richard Evonitz shot and killed himself after a 100 mph car chase from Manatee County ended on Bayfront Drive across from Maria Jack in Sarasota, Florida, on June 27, 2002. (USA TODAY Network via Reuters Connect)
Today, Chamberlain still wonders whether Evonitz had other victims.
"I genuinely believe that he was responsible for more than we know of," she said. "But unfortunately, having taken his own life, that, at this point, is still a mystery."
Chamberlain's own unanswered questions have also shaped how she thinks about families who are still searching for their loved ones.
Kara Robinson Chamberlain hopes the cases featured in "Somebody Knows Something" will generate fresh leads and ultimately help bring them to a close. (ABC News Studios/Freeform)
SIGN UP TO GET THE LATEST TRUE CRIME NEWS
"I think the biggest misconception is that these families will be able to get closure one day," she said of the series.

"I hear people say, 'Let's get these families closure' all the time. And at the end of the day, these people are always going to have some level of trauma. If their loved ones are recovered, they're going to look at a future where they are trying to support that person. If their loved ones are not recovered, they're never found, or unfortunately, they're found, and they're deceased, then they're looking at the rest of their lives missing someone they love."
"That's the biggest thing for me, closure really is a myth," she added.

Kara Robinson Chamberlain forged strong ties with law enforcement and graduated from the South Carolina Criminal Justice Academy. She ultimately joined the same agency that investigated her abduction, serving as a school resource officer, sex crimes and child abuse investigator, and victim advocate until the birth of her children. (ABC News Studios/Freeform)
LIKE WHAT YOU'RE READING? CLICK HERE FOR MORE
In 2010, Chamberlain completed training at the South Carolina Criminal Justice Academy and began working for the Richland County Sheriff's Department as a school resource officer, WIS-TV reported.
SEND US A TIP
That experience helped Chamberlain while filming the series and speaking with families, including a grieving father.
GOT A TIP?
"These people at the center of these stories are more than this story that we know," Chamberlain explained. "They're more than how they disappeared or what happened to them."

If you have information about any of the cases featured in "Somebody Knows Something," contact the appropriate law enforcement agency. Even the smallest detail could help investigators find the answers these families have been waiting for. (ABC News Studios/Freeform)
LISTEN TO THE NEW 'CRIME & JUSTICE WITH DONNA ROTUNNO' PODCAST

"I remember thinking, 'I have so many questions to ask this man,'" she recalled. "[I'm] looking at him and saying, 'This is a man that's heartbroken, who doesn't know what happened to his daughter. He wants to talk about who she was, so I'm going to step back, and I'm going to let him do that.'"
GET BREAKING NEWS BY EMAIL
Chamberlain said her 15-year-old self wouldn't have been surprised by the work she does today.
"Somebody Knows Something" airs Mondays at 9 p.m. on Freeform and streams the next day on Hulu and Hulu on Disney+. (ABC News Studios/Freeform)

"She would've said, 'I knew it,'" Chamberlain said. "She would've known it because I think from very early on, I thought that I was able to handle what happened to me the way that I was able to handle it for a reason. Yes, I had this bad thing that happened to me, but that just became part of building who I became. That's not who I am. It's just a part of my story."
Stephanie Nolasco is an Entertainment Reporter for Fox News Digital.

title: Routine California traffic stop leads to seizure of 30 pounds of cocaine worth more than $800K
summary: A California Highway Patrol canine officer stopped a Honda CR-V in Merced County and allegedly found 30 pounds of suspected cocaine worth $817,200.
story: Anti-narcotics agents in Ecuador seize just over 1,000 pounds of cocaine bricks bearing stickers of Norwegian soccer star Erling Haaland from a false bottom in a truck bed (Credit: Ecuador National Police/AP Newsroom).
California authorities seized more than $800,000 worth of suspected cocaine during a traffic stop this week, officials said.
The California Highway Patrol said a Central Division canine officer stopped a 2025 Honda CR-V in Merced County on Aug. 12 for an alleged traffic violation.
During the stop, the officer identified "several indicators of possible criminal activity," according to CHP.
A subsequent search of the vehicle allegedly uncovered a bag containing approximately 30 pounds of suspected cocaine with an estimated street value of $817,200, CHP said.
TWO SUSPECTS ARRESTED AFTER CRASHING THROUGH CAMP PENDLETON GATE WITH 112 POUNDS OF COCAINE AND FENTANYL
California Highway Patrol officers seized approximately 30 pounds of suspected cocaine with an estimated street value of $817,200 during a traffic stop in Merced County. (California Highway Patrol)

The driver was arrested and booked into the Merced County Main Jail on charges of possession of cocaine for sale and transportation of cocaine across non-contiguous counties, according to authorities.
The Merced Area Gang Narcotics Enforcement Team (MAGNET) is handling the investigation.

The seizure comes after federal authorities last month uncovered more than 1,000 pounds of cocaine hidden beneath the floorboards of a commercial truck entering the U.S. from Mexico, marking one of the largest drug busts in Southern California this year.
FEDS SEIZE $6.4M WORTH OF COCAINE ABOARD OIL TANKER AT PORT OF LOS ANGELES, ARREST SUSPECTED CARTEL SMUGGLER

A California Highway Patrol officer stopped a 2025 Honda CR-V for an alleged traffic violation before allegedly discovering $817,200 worth of suspected cocaine inside the vehicle. (California Highway Patrol)

According to the Justice Department, more than a half-ton of cocaine was discovered concealed in the floorboards of a truck and flatbed trailer at the Calexico Port of Entry along the California-Mexico border. Authorities estimated the cocaine had a street value exceeding $20 million.
U.S. Customs and Border Protection (CBP) also announced last month that officers discovered more than $3.7 million worth of cocaine concealed in a shipment of cucumbers.

title: Alaska runner hospitalized after using bear spray to fight off brown bear on Alaska trail
summary: A runner on Anchorage's Wolverine Bowl trail used bear spray to fend off a brown bear and was hospitalized, marking the second attack in the area in weeks.
story: A woman is recovering after a sudden brown bear encounter in Anchorage on July 18, led officers to deploy a drone while firefighters evacuated her down a hillside. (Anchorage Police)
A runner was hospitalized in Alaska after fending off a bear attack in Anchorage this week.
The woman, who was running by herself at Prospect Heights’ Wolverine Bowl trail, was able to get away from the brown bear by using her bear spray, according to the Alaska Department of Fish and Game.
She was taken to a local hospital for treatment.
BEAR ATTACK IN YELLOWSTONE NATIONAL PARK LEAVES 2 HIKERS INJURED
A woman was hospitalized in Alaska after fending off a bear attack this week. (LightRocket via Getty Images, File)
Biologists went to the site of the attack and collected samples but no bears were seen.
The department said anyone who sees a bear or another wild animal acting aggressively or unusually should report it.
Warning signs have been posted at the Prospect Heights trailhead, the departmet said, adding that hikers should stay off closed trails.

"Thick, dense summer foliage can block sightlines, making surprise encounters more likely," the department said. "Choose hiking routes with good visibility and away from known attractants, like salmon-bearing streams."

When hiking in bear country, people should carry a deterrent such as bear spray or a firearm, stay in groups, make noise to avoid surprising a bear, stay alert for signs of bears, don’t approach bears and keep pets on a leash.
WOMAN ATTACKED BY BROWN BEAR WHILE HIKING WITH FRIEND AND 3 DOGS NEAR ALASKA STATE PARK
A view of the downtown skyline in Anchorage, Alaska. (Getty Images)

"If you surprise a bear, especially one with cubs or on a food cache, it may react in a threatened or defensive manner," the department said. "The bear may be agitated and may huff, stomp, make a popping sound with its teeth, salivate or lay its ears back against its head and charge."
They urged staying calm, standing your ground, readying deterrent, staying in a group and talking calmly. Never run.

"If the bear is stationary, move away slowly while keeping your eyes on the bear," the department said. "If the bear starts to move toward you or charges, stop and stand your ground. Let the bear know you are not a threat. Behaving calmly, moving slowly, and speaking in a low calm voice will help de-escalate the situation. If the bear continues to approach, use your deterrent when the bear is within range."
WOMAN STALKED BY CHARGING BEAR ON MORNING DOG WALK CAPTURES TERRIFYING ENCOUNTER ON CAMERA
The attack comes less than a month after another woman was mauled by a bear in Anchorage.
The attack comes less than a month after another woman was mauled by a bear in Anchorage. (LightRocket via Getty Images, File)
The July victim was walking with a friend and her three dogs in the Bear Valley residential neighborhood, adjacent to Chugach State Park in south Anchorage, when the bear approached.

Officials said the hikers were on an unofficial, user-made trail that climbs a steep hillside in a zigzag pattern. The area was heavily overgrown with dense vegetation, which created poor visibility and increased the risk of surprising wildlife, the department said.

"The bear came out of the dense alders, made brief contact with one of the hikers, and left the scene," the department added.
The woman suffered non-life-threatening injuries and was expected to recover.

title: Nevada man funneled 140 guns to violent Mexican drug cartels, including powerful 'military-style' rifles: DOJ
summary: Luis Alberto Osorio admitted to buying 140 firearms, including military-style rifles for violent Mexican drug-trafficking organizations, in a straw purchase scheme.
story: Acting Attorney General Todd Blanche has announced law enforcement actions against the Jalisco New Generation Cartel for importing fentanyl into the U.S., operating a timeshare fraud scheme and more.

A Nevada man pleaded guilty on Friday to purchasing high-powered firearms and ammunition to sell to drug-trafficking organizations in Mexico, money laundering and employing people illegally in the U.S., Department of Justice officials said.

Luis Alberto Osorio allegedly conspired with co-defendants between April 2020 and last September to buy 140 firearms, magazines, and ammunition for people affiliated with violent Mexican drug-trafficking cartels, which would be sold south of the border for a profit, according to the U.S. Attorney’s Office in Nevada.

The guns included large caliber and long-range firearms such as the Ohio Ordnance Works M2-SLR .50 BMG, the Barrett M82A1 and M107A1 .50 BMG antimaterial rifles, the FN Herstal M249S 5.56x45mm and the FH Herstal SCAR 17S 7.62x51mm rifles, according to court documents.
Osorio also admitted to employing people in the U.S. illegally at a mining company in Nevada.
BORDER AGENTS UNCOVER RPG LAUNCHER, CACHE OF RIFLES HIDDEN IN VEHICLE HEADING TO MEXICO

According to court documents, Osorio conspired with co-defendants between April 2020 and last September to buy 140 firearms, magazines and ammunition for people allegedly affiliated with violent Mexican drug-trafficking cartels. (Getty Images, File)

Osorio, of Elko, pleaded guilty to one count of straw purchasing of firearms; one count of trafficking in firearms; one count of harboring certain aliens; and one count of conspiracy to launder money.
He faces a maximum of 70 years in prison.

"Firearms trafficking networks feed the violent cartels that terrorize border communities and pump illicit drugs into our neighborhoods," First Assistant U.S. Attorney Sigal Chattah for the District of Nevada said in a statement. "By cutting off this supply chain and holding this defendant accountable, we are directly disrupting the operational capabilities of these dangerous criminal organizations."
FBI CHARGES 35 IN WEST VIRGINIA DRUG AND FIREARMS OPERATION, LAUNCHES NATIONWIDE SUMMER CRIME INITIATIVE
Osario’s sentencing is scheduled for February.

"Trafficking military-style firearms and ammunition to drug trafficking organizations in Mexico fuels violence, strengthens criminal networks and threatens communities on both sides of the border," said Jonathan Sherwin, deputy special agent in charge of Homeland Security Investigations (HSI) Las Vegas. "This guilty plea is the result of relentless work by HSI and the Homeland Security Task Force and our federal, state and local partners to disrupt the flow of weapons, money and criminal support that allows these organizations to operate."
A burned truck is seen as members of the Civil Guard of Michoacan patrol a highway after a wave of cartel violence in Aguililla, Mexico. (AFP via Getty Images, File)
The case is part of the Homeland Security Task Force initiative, which was created by an executive order President Donald Trump signed on his first day in office last year.

"In the world of organized crime and drug trafficking, guns and drugs go hand-in-hand," David S. Olesky, special agent in charge of the Drug Enforcement Administration Los Angeles Field Division, which covers Nevada, said in a statement.

"As a member of the Homeland Security Task Force, DEA and our partners will bring to bear all resources and draw on the full scope of our agencies’ expertise to hold accountable those individuals and organizations which pose a public health and safety threat to our communities through the trafficking of drugs and firearms."

title: Ex-detective who served fraction of 102-year sentence faces new charges after cold case review
summary: Former Los Angeles vice detective Michael Douglas Brambles, paroled in 2020 under California's elderly inmates law, faces new kidnapping charges.
story: Fox News Flash top headlines are here. Check out what's clicking on Foxnews.com.

A former Los Angeles vice detective who was sentenced to 102 years in prison three decades ago for multiple rapes but paroled in 2020, because of a California law was arrested again this week, authorities said.

Michael Douglas Brambles, 77, is charged with kidnapping to commit robbery while personally using a firearm in connection with an alleged robbery and sexual assault, according to the Ventura County District Attorney’s Office.

He also faces several aggravating circumstances, "including that the crime involved great violence, the victim was particularly vulnerable, the manner in which the crime was carried out indicated planning, sophistication or professionalism, and that Brambles engaged in violent conduct indicating a serious danger to society," the district attorney’s office said.
CALIFORNIA SUED OVER POLICY THAT COULD FREE SERIAL KILLERS AS LACI PETERSON'S FRIEND SOUNDS ALARM

Michael Douglas Brambles, 77, is charged with kidnapping to commit robbery while personally using a firearm in connection with an alleged robbery and sexual assault, according to the Ventura County District Attorney’s Office. (Ventura County District Attorney's Office; Lou Benoist/ AFP via Getty Images)

Brambles allegedly entered Arabella’s Boutique in Thousand Oaks, California, when a woman identified as SW was closing, pointed a handgun at her, and forced her into the backroom where he tied her hands behind her back and sexually assaulted her.
He is also accused of stealing from the business before he left.
The sexual assault allegations cannot be charged because the statute of limitations has passed.
Shortly after the crime, Brambles was identified as a suspect, but he was already being prosecuted for a string of robberies and sexual assaults.
He was convicted on 26 counts, including 18 armed robberies and multiple sexual assaults.
After being sentenced to 102 years, SW’s case was dismissed, which she agreed with, believing he would spend the rest of his life in prison.
But he was able to apply for parole in 2020 under a California law that allows elderly inmates to apply.
NEWSOM-BACKED LAW LETS ILLEGAL IMMIGRANT CHILD RAPIST SEEK EARLY RELEASE AGAIN AS DA URGES 'STOP THE MADNESS'
Victim SW speaks at the Ventura County District Attorney's Office press conference this week. (Ventura County District Attorney's Office)
At his parole hearing, Brambles denied sexually assaulting any women besides the cases he had already been convicted for in Los Angeles County.
While examining SW’s cold case as part of the federal Sexual Assault Kit Initiative, Ventura County District Attorney’s Office investigators realized he had been paroled.
Brambles was arrested on Wednesday and is being held in Ventura County on $2 million bail.

"A few months ago, when investigators from the Ventura County District Attorney’s Office contacted me, I was shocked to hear not only that this man was walking free, but that he had been out of prison for six years," SW said at a press conference this week. "The justice that I and his other victims deserved was denied when he was only required to serve a fraction of the sentence he earned. I am thankful to have this opportunity now to seek justice for myself and for his other victims."
HOUSE DEMOCRAT BLASTED AFTER EARLY RELEASE LAW FREED INMATES LATER CHARGED WITH MURDER
The Ventura County District Attorney's office in California. (Ventura County District Attorny's Office/Facebook)
Brambles faces a maximum sentence of 12 years to life if convicted.

A Florida middle school teacher was arrested after investigators said he exchanged inappropriate messages with a former teenage student and acknowledged communicating inappropriately with the student since 2023.
Christian Schneider, 31, a teacher at Memorial Middle School, was arrested Friday on charges of three felonies following an investigation by the Hillsborough County Sheriff's Office.

HIGH SCHOOL COUNSELOR PLEADS GUILTY TO MULTIPLE SEX CRIMES INVOLVING TEEN SHE WAS MEANT TO HELP

A Florida man charged in the 1987 killing of a 20-year-old mother allegedly confessed after contacting authorities himself, and investigators say he described details of the crime that had never been publicly released.

Gary Edward Glowacz, 70, was charged with second-degree murder and armed burglary with assault or battery in the death of Melissa Ellison, who was found dead inside her Jacksonville home Dec. 28, 1987, according to court records obtained by Fox News Digital.
Ellison was found lying on her bed after her roommates first discovered her 13-month-old child crying on a couch in the living room, according to Glowacz’s arrest report.

Melissa Ellison's body was found by authorities in her bed with injuries consistent with blunt force trauma, according to police. (Jacksonville County Sheriff's Office)
The case remained unsolved for decades.

title: Police announce arrest after 5 wounded in Virginia State University shooting: report
summary: Multiple victims were transported to area hospitals Saturday morning after a shooting near the Quad Annexes at Virginia State University, campus police says.
story: The ‘Fox & Friends Weekend’ panel gives the latest on a reported shooting at Virginia State University.
At least five people were shot at Virginia State University (VSU) Saturday morning, and one remains in critical condition, according to university officials and the VSU Police Department.
Police arrested 19-year-old Camron Harris of Henrico, Virginia, on Saturday after finding him hiding in a dormitory closet on campus in connection with the shooting, The Associated Press reported.
Harris is not a VSU student, Chesterfield County Police said.

Police obtained eight felony warrants in connection with the case, including for malicious wounding and use of a firearm in the commission of a felony, according to the AP. It was not immediately clear whether Harris had an attorney who could speak on his behalf.

"Officers responded to the 3300 block of Boisseau Street at approximately 1:28 a.m. and discovered five individuals suffering from gunshot wounds outside VSU residence halls," a university official told Fox News Digital.
STUDENT PERPETRATES DEADLY SHOOTING AT THAILAND HIGH SCHOOL, AUTHORITIES SAY
There has been a massive police presence on the Virginia State University campus after an early morning shooting. (WRLH-WWBT)
"All five were transported to area hospitals. One individual is currently in critical condition. The remaining four sustained non-life-threatening injuries."
The university said earlier on X that the shooting involved "multiple suspects." No arrests have been announced.
Police had not provided additional information Saturday evening about whether authorities were still searching for other suspects.
VSU, a state-supported HBCU, is located in Ettrick, Virginia, about 25 miles south of Richmond.
HOUSTON POLICE SHOOT GUNMAN WHO INDISCRIMINATELY FIRED ON VEHICLES, INJURING A MOTHER AND DAUGHTER
A street on Virginia State University's campus Saturday, after at least five people were shot early in the morning. (WRLH-WWBT)

One of the victims was confirmed to be a VSU student. The student was among those who sustained non-life-threatening injuries and has been released from a hospital, the university said in a statement.
Police said the five people who were shot range in age from 17 to 23. Four are not VSU students. The VSU student is 20 years old. The victims' names have not been released.
Authorities have not disclosed a possible motive.
VSU police earlier revealed that the shooting occurred near the school's Quad Annexes student housing complex.
SEVERAL PEOPLE DEAD, INCLUDING SUSPECT, IN RURAL MICHIGAN MULTI-SCENE SHOOTING: POLICE
According to the university, law enforcement "does not believe there is an immediate threat to the VSU campus community."

"We recognize the concern this incident has caused among our students, parents, alumni, friends and the broader VSU community," the university said in a statement Saturday afternoon. "VSU police will maintain an increased presence on campus as the investigation continues.
"Students should monitor their VSU email for additional safety measures currently in effect and information about available support resources."
The campus initially went into lockdown, but the lockdown has been lifted, according to a university official and VSU police.

The shooting occurred on the same day that resident halls opened to returning students Friday for the school's fall 2026 semester, according to the school's calendar. Classes for the semester will begin on Monday.
Rozia A. Henson Jr., a Democratic member of the Virginia House of Delegates, shared a message on social media praying for the victims and their families.

"Virginia State University is my alma mater. Waking up to this news is heartbreaking. My prayers are with everyone affected this morning, with their families, and with the entire Trojan family. VSU, we are with you," Henson Jr. posted on X.

Virginia Gov. Abigail Spanberger also addressed the shooting in a social media post Saturday afternoon, saying she and her husband "are praying for a quick recovery for those who were shot this morning at Virginia State University."
"Our thoughts are with the VSU community. Thank you to the first responders and law enforcement who responded to the scene," she wrote.

An investigation into the shooting, led by the Chesterfield County Police Department with assistance from VSU police, U.S. Alcohol Tobacco & Firearms (ATF), and the Hanover County Sheriff's Office, is ongoing, a university official told Fox News Digital.
