title: Killer ex-cop executed for child's slaying as sheriff says he’s sure same monster murdered another girl
summary: James Duckett's execution brought closure to two families who believe the former police officer killed both Teresa McAbee and Jeanifer Weldon in 1987.
story: James Duckett was executed for the 1987 rape and murder of 11-year-old Teresa McAbee. Investigators believe he also killed Jeanifer Weldon that same year. (Credit: WTVT)
After almost four decades, the execution of James Duckett brought closure for two families who believe they both lost young girls to the same killer.
The 68-year-old was executed by lethal injection July 28 for the rape and murder of 11-year-old Teresa McAbee while on duty as a cop for the Mascotte Police Department.
McAbee’s family attended his execution at the Florida State Prison in Raiford.
They were joined by family and friends of 14-year-old Jeanifer Weldon. Authorities believe she also was killed by Duckett four months after he murdered McAbee.
INVESTIGATORS REVISIT FLORIDA SERIAL KILLER CASE AS SEARCH RESUMES FOR POSSIBLE ADDITIONAL VICTIMS
Investigators believe Jeanifer Weldon (L) was killed by James Duckett (R) in Fort Meade, Fla., in September 1987. (Polk County Sheriff’s Office)
But law enforcement officials stopped pursuing a conviction out of fear it would prolong his life, Polk County Sheriff Grady Judd said in a news conference.

It had been decided that piecing together evidence on the case could "jam up" the process or "create more defense, or more arguments, or more excuses why he shouldn't be executed," Judd told reporters on July 30.
So once Duckett was sentenced to die for McAbee’s murder, authorities stopped pushing to secure a conviction for the killing of Weldon, Judd said.
Two lives lost
McAbee went missing in May 1987. She was last seen with Duckett in his patrol car on an evening when he was the only officer working the streets.
When her body was found, evidence showed she’d been sexually assaulted, strangled and drowned, according to court records.
A month later, Duckett was named a suspect and was fired from his job as a cop. Very strong fingerprint and DNA evidence linked Duckett to the case, Judd said.
NEW CALIFORNIA LAW EXPANDS DNA TOOLS FOR MISSING PERSONS INVESTIGATIONS
Authorities found Weldon’s body in a wooded area behind the road where her shoes were found. (Polk County Sheriff’s Office)
Then three months later, another girl went missing in Central Florida.
Weldon disappeared on Sept. 19, 1987, in Polk County, about an hour south of the town where Duckett had worked as a police officer.
It was three days before her 15th birthday.
She’d spent the Saturday with friends on a trip to town to Tampa, where she’d bought a fluffy kitten to add to the stuffed animal collection in her bedroom, Judd said.
Around 9 p.m., she left her friends to walk about two miles home, carrying her new stuffed kitten in a green plastic bag, Judd said. She never made it home.

For "13 frantic days, we looked for Jeanifer to no avail," Judd told reporters almost 39 years later. There were few leads, until a phosphate miner pulled over to investigate a pair of shoes he spotted on the side of the road in Fort Meade. It had been about two weeks since Weldon had disappeared.
When he got out of his car, he was hit with the pungent smell of a decomposing body, Judd said.
Weldon’s "skeletonized" remains were found behind tall grass and a berm in a wooded area away from the road, Judd said.
Duckett eventually became a suspect in that killing, too.
Investigators believed Duckett had used his old law enforcement uniform to convince Weldon he could provide a safe ride home.
Family members and investigators felt Weldon wouldn’t have gotten in a car with Duckett without that reassurance and confidence that he was a police officer and someone she could trust, Judd said.
She died by strangulation, he said.
Investigators suspect she was raped before her death.
A heartbreaking clue
A month after Weldon’s death, Duckett was arrested for the killing and sexual battery of McAbee.
He quickly became a suspect in Weldon’s killing, too. But the evidence wasn’t as strong, and was more circumstantial, Judd said.
The night Weldon disappeared, Duckett had left for work at his new mining job five hours early. He drove down the highway "exactly past where Jeanifer Weldon would have been walking home," Judd said.

He arrived at work sweaty and two hours late, saying that he’d had car trouble. But investigators learned that his hands weren't "greasy or nasty or dirty," Judd said. The next day, Duckett brought home a gift for his children—a stuffed kitten in a green plastic bag.
It matched the one purchased by Weldon.

Weldon kept a collection of stuffed animals in her bedroom, and her last planned addition provided a clue for investigators looking for her killer. (Polk County Sheriff’s Office)

Polk County investigators spent tens of thousands of hours working to pursue a conviction in the Weldon case, Judd said.
Then a few years ago, after Duckett was convicted of McAbee’s murder and had received the death sentence, they questioned whether they should continue pursuing it, he said.

title: Man charged with assault, hate crimes after allegedly disrupting Shabbat services at NYC synagogue
summary: Larry Montes is facing multiple charges after allegedly striking a congregant and headbutting a security team member during Shabbat services at Central Synagogue in New York City.
story: Fox News Flash top headlines are here. Check out what's clicking on FoxNews.com.

A man was charged with multiple hate crimes after allegedly disrupting Shabbat services at a New York City synagogue Friday, striking a congregant and attacking a member of the security team, authorities said.
New York City Police Commissioner Jessica Tisch said the man disrupted services at Central Synagogue on Lexington Avenue in Manhattan.

The NYPD later identified the suspect as Larry Montes, 46, of the Bronx, and said he was charged with two counts of assault as a hate crime and one count of criminal mischief as a hate crime, among other charges.
NORTH CAROLINA WOMAN CHARGED IN ALLEGED HOUSTON SYNAGOGUE ATTACK PLOT AS INVESTIGATORS SEARCH FOR 2 OTHERS

A Bronx man was charged with multiple hate crimes after allegedly disrupting Shabbat services and attacking a congregant and security member at Central Synagogue in Manhattan, police said. (REUTERS/Eduardo Munoz)

"As synagogue security was escorting him out, he struck a member of the congregation, damaged synagogue property, and then spit at and headbutted a member of the security team," Tisch said in a statement posted on X.
An NYPD sergeant working a paid detail at the synagogue immediately intervened and took Montes into custody, according to Tisch.
No one was seriously injured, and the incident remains under investigation, Tisch said.

"I have spoken with the rabbi of the synagogue, and I'm relieved that no one was seriously injured," she said. "Those who were hurt were evaluated at the scene and are doing well. There are no known additional threats at this time, and additional NYPD resources have been deployed to the synagogue."
JEWISH LEADERS FAULT MAMDANI RHETORIC AS UPPER WEST SIDE STABBING, HATE CRIME PROBE CONTINUES
NYPD Commissioner Jessica Tisch said no one was seriously injured during the alleged attack at Central Synagogue, which she said was the synagogue where she grew up. (WNYW)
New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani said he was "horrified" by the incident.
"I am horrified by the assault at Central Synagogue during services today," Mamdani said.

"I can only imagine the pain and fear an attack like this, during Shabbat services, causes for the congregation and for Jewish New Yorkers across our city," he continued. "Every New Yorker must be able to observe their religion without fear of violence."
"This despicable act has no place in our city, and our administration will do everything in our power to keep Jewish New Yorkers safe," he added.
New York Gov. Kathy Hochul also condemned the alleged attack.

"What happened at Central Synagogue tonight is appalling," Hochul posted on X. "Jewish New Yorkers have every right to worship openly, proudly, and without fear. I’m grateful the suspect is in custody and that no one was seriously injured."
Tisch said the incident was particularly personal because she grew up attending Central Synagogue.

title: Shake Shack worker allegedly calls out before robbing own restaurant, returns in uniform 2 days later
summary: An Arizona Shake Shack employee allegedly robbed his own restaurant at gunpoint, locked co-workers in a cooler, then returned in uniform two days later.
story: A viral video shows a Shake Shack kiosk increasing the price of an order after a customer selected the option to decline a tip. The company responded by attributing the price change to a technology error.

An Arizona Shake Shack employee is facing charges after allegedly robbing his own restaurant at gunpoint, locking two co-workers in a walk-in cooler and then returning to work in uniform just two days later.

Keondre Simmons, 33, allegedly called out of work at the Shake Shack at Kierland Commons in Phoenix around midnight on Aug. 3 before showing up at the restaurant later that morning to commit the robbery, according to court documents reviewed by FOX 10 Phoenix.
Investigators responding to the armed robbery learned that an employee opened a rear delivery door after hearing a bell and believing a scheduled delivery had arrived.
CHICK-FIL-A EMPLOYEE BUSTED IN BIZARRE $80K MAC-AND-CHEESE THEFT SCHEME

Keondre Simmons, 33, is accused of robbing the Shake Shack where he worked at gunpoint before returning to the restaurant in uniform two days later, according to court documents. (Maricopa County Sheriff's Office; iStock)
"[The employee] opened the door after hearing the delivery bell, believing a scheduled delivery had arrived," court documents state.

"When the door opened, the suspect pointed a firearm at [the employee], ordered him inside, and escorted him at gunpoint toward the walk-in cooler. The suspect forced [the employee] inside and locked the cooler door."
Police said the suspect then forced the on-duty manager into the office and ordered him to open the store's safe.

"[The on-duty manager] unlocked the safe and, under threat of firearm, removed approximately $2,800 in mixed denominations and placed it into a black gun case-style container the suspect carried," police wrote. "The suspect subsequently forced [the on-duty manager] into the walk-in cooler with [the employee], and successfully locked the door."

Investigators said both victims eventually managed to escape the cooler, but the suspect returned moments later, escorted them to the office and ordered them to kneel at gunpoint.

"The suspect took both victims' cellphones and the office landline, then destroyed them by throwing them into a sink filled with water. The suspect then exited the business through the rear delivery door," police wrote.
Investigators later identified Simmons as the suspect, according to the court documents.
Two days after the robbery, Simmons allegedly returned to the Shake Shack wearing his work uniform, where police arrested him.

A Shake Shack employee allegedly stole approximately $2,800 from the restaurant at Kierland Commons in Phoenix after holding two co-workers at gunpoint, according to court documents. (iStock)
Simmons later told investigators that he "discarded the clothing worn during the incident, and a firearm is inside his residence," according to court documents.
Simmons faces charges of armed robbery, aggravated assault and kidnapping.

title: Delta flight diverted twice after lavatory leak floods cabin, leaves passengers stranded for hours
summary: Delta Air Lines Flight 81 declared an emergency for an overweight landing at Heathrow after a lavatory issue forced the Paris-to-Seattle diversion.
story: A routine maintenance test flight over northwest England drew widespread attention after its flight path appeared to spell out 'I'm bored' on the Flightradar24 flight-tracking website.
A Delta Air Lines flight traveling from Paris to Seattle made an unexpected stop in London after the crew reported a mechanical issue involving an onboard lavatory, the airline said.
Delta Flight 81 departed Paris-Charles de Gaulle Airport Aug. 13 bound for Seattle-Tacoma International Airport when the issue prompted the flight crew to divert to London Heathrow Airport.
The Airbus A330-900 was carrying 209 passengers and 13 crew members at the time, according to information provided by Delta.
As the aircraft approached Heathrow, the flight crew declared an emergency with air traffic control because the plane would be making an overweight landing, the airline said.
FLAMES SHOOT FROM AMERICAN AIRLINES FLIGHT BEFORE EMERGENCY LANDING

A Delta Air Lines aircraft taxis at London Heathrow Airport in London Oct. 7, 2016. Delta Flight 81 diverted to Heathrow after its crew reported a mechanical issue involving an onboard lavatory. (Simon Dawson/Bloomberg via Getty Images)
Despite the emergency declaration, the aircraft landed normally and safely at Heathrow.
Delta maintenance personnel then serviced the Airbus in London in an effort to address the lavatory-related mechanical issue.

"We apologize to our customers for their experience and delay on Delta Flight 81 from Paris-Charles de Gaulle to Seattle, which diverted to London Heathrow after the crew reported a mechanical issue involving an onboard lavatory," a Delta spokesperson said in a statement to Fox News Digital.
"This is not the experience we strive to provide, and we're focused on getting our customers to their destinations as quickly and safely as possible."
LIVE BULLET FOUND ABOARD UNITED FLIGHT FORCES PASSENGERS OFF PLANE FOR SECURITY SWEEP AT DENVER AIRPORT

A Delta Air Lines Airbus A330-900, registration N812NW, is pictured at Leonardo da Vinci – Fiumicino Airport in Italy July 8, 2025. Delta Flight 81 was operated by an Airbus A330-900 carrying 209 passengers and 13 crew members when it diverted to London. (Massimo Insabato/Archivio Massimo Insabato/Mondadori Portfolio via Getty Images)
Once maintenance work was completed, the aircraft departed Heathrow, but the disruption meant passengers still faced an additional detour before reaching their intended destination on the West Coast.
Instead of continuing directly from London to Seattle, the flight headed to New York's John F. Kennedy International Airport because of the crew's available duty time, according to Delta.
Passengers cleared U.S. Customs at JFK before continuing their journey to Seattle.
The unusual itinerary ultimately took the 209 passengers from Paris to London, then across the Atlantic to New York before they could continue on to Seattle.

Passengers prepare to board a flight at London Heathrow Airport June 27, 2026. Delta Flight 81 made an unscheduled stop at Heathrow while traveling from Paris to Seattle after its crew reported a mechanical issue. (Marc Fernandes/NurPhoto via Getty Images)

In an update on Saturday afternoon, police revealed the ages and genders of the victims.

At around 11:40 a.m. local time Friday, state troopers were dispatched to a home on South LaChance Road in Lake Township, where they found three people who had been killed, including a 45-year-old man, 40-year-old woman and 16-year-old boy.

During the "large-scale" search for Hickman, police found a fourth body at another home in Missaukee County belonging to a 53-year-old man, authorities said.
State police said Hickman's car was seen near a wooded area where his body, along with the body of a 29-year-old woman were later found.

title: FBI captures Top Ten Most Wanted fugitive with alleged Sinaloa Cartel ties, Patel says
summary: Gregory Henderson Jr. was captured three days after being added to the FBI Ten Most Wanted list for alleged drug trafficking tied to the Sinaloa Cartel.
story: Los Angeles Police Department Chief Jim McDonnell says authorities are now offering a $1 million reward for Omar Alexander Cardenas, a suspect on the FBI’s Ten Most Wanted Fugitives list. (KTTV)

The FBI captured Ten Most Wanted fugitive Gregory Henderson Jr., just three days after adding the alleged Indianapolis gang leader to its list and offering a reward of up to $1 million for information leading to his arrest.

Henderson, 46, had evaded arrest since a sweeping federal takedown of his alleged organization in August 2023. He faces federal charges of conspiracy to possess with intent to distribute and to distribute controlled substances, conspiracy to launder monetary instruments and conspiracy to engage in an animal fighting venture.

The FBI alleges Henderson led a violent Indianapolis gang whose drug trafficking network was supplied by the Sinaloa Cartel and distributed methamphetamine, cocaine and fentanyl throughout Indianapolis and the surrounding Midwest.
WOMAN ADDED TO FBI'S TEN MOST WANTED LIST ARRESTED HOURS LATER AFTER TIPS POURED IN FROM FLORIDA: PATEL
The FBI marked Gregory Henderson Jr.’s Ten Most Wanted Fugitives poster "CAPTURED" following his arrest. (FBI)

His capture marks the ninth FBI Ten Most Wanted fugitive apprehended since President Donald Trump returned to office. The nine fugitives had collectively spent more than 50 years on the run, according to the FBI. The FBI says the nine captures are more than twice the four Ten Most Wanted fugitives captured during the Biden administration.
FBI Director Kash Patel told Fox News Digital exclusively that Henderson’s capture reflected a broader increase in Ten Most Wanted apprehensions under the Trump administration.

"Nine Top Ten Most Wanted Fugitives is more than twice as many as captured under the entirety of the prior administration — and this FBI and our partners did it in 18 months under President Trump’s brilliant leadership," Patel said. "Gregory Henderson Jr. had been on the run for a year, wanted for his alleged involvement in major drug trafficking operation and animal fighting conspiracies as the alleged leader of a violent neighborhood-based gang located in Indianapolis, Indiana - a gang with significant drug distribution ties to the Sinaloa Cartel."

"This administration is letting good cops be cops and they are delivering in historic ways. I’d like to congratulate our FBI Indianapolis team who led this case from the beginning and thank our great Justice Department and law enforcement partners who righteously pursued this case with us," he added.
'AMERICA'S MOST WANTED' FUGITIVE CAPTURED ON SAILBOAT OFF NJ COAST AFTER 20 YEARS ON THE RUN
Gregory Henderson Jr. was captured after being added to the FBI’s Ten Most Wanted Fugitives list on Aug. 11. (FBI)
The U.S. Department of Agriculture’s Office of Inspector General was among the federal partners involved in the case.

"I would like to thank the FBI, DOJ, and our USDA OIG among many other federal partners in their relentless pursuit for justice. Mr. Henderson had sought to evade the law after committing multiple crimes and leaving behind pain and anguish for many people and animals, but today is the end of that devastation," U.S. Secretary of Agriculture Brooke L. Rollins told Fox News Digital "President Trump has focused his administration on delivering justice for those targeted by violent crimes, and we will not rest until we achieve this goal."
The FBI added Henderson to its Ten Most Wanted Fugitives list on Aug. 11, describing him as armed and dangerous.

Henderson and 20 others were federally indicted in the Southern District of Indiana in August 2023 on drug trafficking and dog fighting conspiracy charges. More than 300 federal, state and local law enforcement officers carried out a takedown later that month, arresting 18 people while Henderson evaded capture.
Federal agents seized 61 guns, quantities of fentanyl, methamphetamine and cocaine, $98,000 in cash and 166 fighting dogs during the operation, according to the FBI.
Law enforcement also uncovered what the FBI described as a significant dog fighting and illegal gambling operation allegedly led by Henderson.

"Henderson Jr. has a long history of criminal activity, including street violence, intimidation, assault, and weapons, in addition to drug trafficking and animal cruelty," said FBI Indianapolis Special Agent in Charge Tim O’Malley.

Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI) Director Kash Patel (C) speaks at a news conference at the Robert F. Kennedy Department of Justice building on June 23, 2026, in Washington, DC. (Anna Moneymaker/Getty Images)

Details about where and how Henderson was captured were not immediately available.

title: Alex Murdaugh defense says murder weapon may be tied to separate killing as judge seeks answers
summary: Jim Griffin claims a recent Allendale County homicide may involve weapons connected to the Murdaugh murders, stunning prosecutors and the judge.
story: Creighton Waters told the court the rifle used in the Allendale County shooting was run through a national gun database and came back with no matches. The defense had suggested a possible tie to the Murdaugh murder weapons.

Alex Murdaugh’s defense attorneys on Friday raised an unverified claim that a recent Allendale County homicide could be connected to the Murdaugh murders, surprising prosecutors and the judge overseeing his retrial.

Murdaugh returned to court after the South Carolina Supreme Court unanimously overturned his 2023 convictions and two life sentences earlier this year for the killings of his wife, Maggie Murdaugh, and son, Paul Murdaugh.

The court found that former Colleton County Clerk of Court Becky Hill improperly influenced jurors, depriving Murdaugh of an impartial jury, and ordered a new trial. Murdaugh remains imprisoned on separate state and federal financial-crime sentences.
ALEX MURDAUGH'S DOUBLE MURDER CONVICTION UNANIMOUSLY OVERTURNED BY SOUTH CAROLINA SUPREME COURT

On Friday, defense attorney Jim Griffin told South Carolina Circuit Court Judge Debra McCaslin that the defense learned through FITSNews reporting that a recent Allendale County murder may have involved weapons connected to the Murdaugh case.
Before August 14, 2026, Alex Murdaugh was last in plainclothes during his financial crimes sentencing on November 28, 2023, at the Beaufort County Courthouse. (Pool)
Griffin said the defense wanted the state to investigate and turn over any related records.

FITSNews told Fox News Digital that Griffin’s reference was to its Aug. 8 "Week in Review" YouTube episode. According to a transcript reviewed by Fox News Digital, FITS founding editor Will Folks and research director Jenn Wood discussed what they described as an unverified report involving a possible third gun at the Moselle crime scene.
ALEX MURDAUGH DEMANDS NEW EVIDENCE SEARCH IN HUNT FOR CRACKS IN CASE
"We’re hearing reports that a Murdaugh gun was used in a subsequent crime," Folks said. "We’re not going to say where at this point. We’re not going to get into the details."

State Judge Debra McCaslin oversees a judicial hearing on Monday, June 29, 2026, at the Marc H. Westbrook Judicial Center in Lexington, South Carolina. Alex Murdaugh will be retried in the June 7, 2021, shooting deaths of his wife and son, after his original conviction was overturned due to jury tampering. (Tracy Glantz/The State via Pool)
Folks said the outlet was investigating whether the firearm was tied to the Murdaugh family and perhaps one of the guns that has never been recovered.
Wood cautioned that the information had not been confirmed.

"It’s a pretty consistent rumor and, you know, I’m hearing it from very good sources," Wood said. "We have not been able to validate a lot of it, and I’m not sure if it’s even the gun. It just said that it was tied to the murder of Maggie and Paul Murdaugh."
ALEX MURDAUGH LAWYERS ALLEGE ‘FABRICATED’ EVIDENCE WAS USED TO SECURE MURDER INDICTMENTS
Neither speaker identified Allendale County, described a ballistics comparison or said investigators had established that a weapon used in the Murdaugh killings was used in a subsequent crime.
The Moselle Estate House in Islandton, which once served as the Murdaugh family's primary residence. (South Carolina State Attorney's Office/Keen Eye Marking)

At Friday’s hearing, Griffin did not identify the victim, the alleged weapon or any testing that supported the purported connection. He said the defense wanted related records as potential Brady material — evidence that could be favorable to the defense.

Griffin told McCaslin that a South Carolina Law Enforcement Division (SLED) firearms examiner testified at Murdaugh’s first trial that shell casings from the .300 Blackout rifle used to kill Maggie Murdaugh bore extraction marks matching casings recovered from the Murdaugh family’s shooting range.
Griffin said that if shell casings from the Allendale County case matched casings tied to the Murdaugh murders, the defense wanted the underlying testing and investigative records.
ALEX MURDAUGH MAKES 'EXPLOSIVE' BID TO BLOW UP MURDER CASE HINGING ON DNA, DIRTY MONEY AND LIES: EXPERT
Such a finding, he argued, could raise questions about the original ballistics analysis or suggest that a firearm associated with the Murdaugh case was later used in another killing.
FOLLOW THE FOX TRUE CRIME TEAM ON X

Creighton Waters, a prosecutor for the S.C. Attorney General’s office, points at Alex Murdaugh in the double murder trial of Alex Murdaugh at the Colleton County Courthouse in Walterboro, Monday, Jan. 30, 2023. (Andrew J. Whitaker/The Post and Courier/Pool)
Lead prosecutor Creighton Waters told the court the allegation was entirely new to him.
"I have never heard the first thing about that," Waters said, adding that he communicates with SLED daily and had not been told of any such development.
"I will certainly look into that, but I would be flabbergasted to find out that actually had happened and no one had advised this office of that," Waters said.
SIGN UP TO GET THE LATEST TRUE CRIME NEWS
McCaslin also appeared struck by the allegation.
LIKE WHAT YOU'RE READING? CLICK HERE FOR MORE
"As far as the murder in Allendale with the murder weapons, you certainly raised my eyebrows on that," McCaslin told Griffin.
Alex Murdaugh is taken to the Colleton County Courthouse for sentencing on March 3, 2023. (Joshua Boucher/Pool/The State/Tribune News Service via Getty Images)
SEND US A TIP
Griffin said FITSNews had broken other Murdaugh-related stories before the defense learned of them. He also told the court that a podcast included a reference to the alleged connection.
GOT A TIP?
McCaslin directed Griffin to send the material to Waters for review.
LISTEN TO THE NEW 'CRIME & JUSTICE WITH DONNA ROTUNNO' PODCAST
Waters said he does not follow podcasts or blogs covering the case.
GET BREAKING NEWS BY EMAIL

"I don’t watch the podcast and I don’t read the blogs because I try to base what I’m doing on the evidence and not on speculation that’s out there in the media," Waters said. "It would blow my mind if something like that had happened in SLED and not call me."

No evidence establishing a connection between an Allendale County homicide and weapons used in the Murdaugh killings has been presented.

Waters later said during Friday's hearing that SLED then told him there is no known ballistics match linking a .300 Blackout used in an Allendale County shooting to another crime. Waters said the firearm evidence from the Allendale case was entered into a ballistics database but "there have been no leads or no matches on that."

"I’m going to find out more and double check, and we’re going to run this down," Waters said, adding that SLED told him there were "no leads or hits" involving the .300 Blackout used in the Allendale shooting.
Fox News Digital's Sarah Rumpf-Whitten contributed to this report.

title: Massachusetts mayor charged with wire fraud in $1.5M COVID relief scheme
summary: Brian DePena allegedly funneled over $1.5 million in EIDL loan funds into his campaign account, personal taxes, and real estate debts, federal charges say.
story: Kayleigh McEnany details the case of Alios Williams, a former federal employee who defrauded the government of over $3.5 million from COVID-era relief. Williams, acting as an SBA loan officer, directly messaged individuals on Instagram, promising to approve fraudulent grant applications in exchange for a fee.

The mayor of a Boston suburb is facing federal wire fraud and money laundering charges for allegedly using more than $1.5 million in pandemic-era small business loans to pad his campaign account, pay personal taxes, and settle high-interest real estate debts.

Lawrence Mayor Brian DePena, 61, was arrested Friday morning following an investigation into his alleged misuse of Economic Injury Disaster Loans (EIDL) — a program administered by the U.S. Small Business Administration (SBA) under the CARES Act to assist struggling businesses during the COVID-19 pandemic.
DePena was elected mayor of Lawrence in November 2021 and won reelection in November 2025. He previously served on the Lawrence City Council from 2016 to 2021.

"Mayor DePena was elected to be a leader for the City of Lawrence," said U.S. Attorney Leah B. Foley. "He was looked up to and trusted by his constituents, but he betrayed that trust through his alleged corruption and lies. Today’s arrest is just another example of our determination to root out fraud by anyone, even public officials, and hold elected officials accountable."
DISGRACED DEM CUT OFF FROM DOING BUSINESS WITH GOVERNMENT AFTER ALLEGED ‘OUTRIGHT FRAUD’ UNCOVERED

Lawrence Mayor Brian DePena faces federal charges for allegedly using pandemic-relief funds meant to assist struggling business for his mayoral campaign and to pay off his personal debts. DePena applied for the funds to help Tenares Tire Services Inc., his tire shop in Lawrence, federal prosecutors said. (City of Lawrence)

In May 2020, DePena applied for an EIDL on behalf of his business, Tenares Tire Service Inc., an auto service and tire shop in Lawrence. The EIDL funds, which carried a 3.75% interest rate, were only to be used to alleviate pandemic-related financial struggles for businesses.

The SBA initially approved a $150,000 loan for Tenares Tire in June 2020. However, DePena sought additional funding months later upon facing cash flow issues. In April 2021, he applied for an increase and was approved for a $350,000 modification. A second loan modification followed in October 2021 that brought the total to $1.1 million.
Upon the second loan modification, DePena was unable to access the funds for a month, resulting in panic, officials said.

"Brother, call me, I’m in trouble. I don’t want to pressure you, but I don’t have time to wait for this loan. I’m in your hands," DePena allegedly wrote in a translated Spanish text message to a financial advisor assisting with the loan application.
"I know I’m bothering you a lot, but I have no other option," he added. "Only you can give me what I need."
ALLEGED FEEDING OUR FUTURE FRAUD RINGLEADER TRANSFERRED FROM SOMALIA TO FACE US CHARGES

Upon receiving the funds, prosecutors claim DePena began diverting them. Between August and October 2021, he allegedly transferred nearly $90,000 from his business accounts to personal accounts, subsequently writing checks totaling over $42,000 directly to "The Committee to Elect Brian DePena".

In addition, officials said he used the taxpayer funds to pay off personal debts, including $85,000 paid to the Internal Revenue Service (IRS) to settle personal back taxes and another $883,293 to pay off high-interest mortgages on personal properties he owned in Lawrence.

"CARES Act funds were created to help small businesses survive an unprecedented national crisis — not to bankroll personal debts, political ambitions, or real estate ventures," said Thomas Demeo, special agent in charge of the IRS Criminal Investigation Boston Field Office. "IRS Criminal Investigation remains committed to protecting taxpayer dollars, pursuing those who exploit federal relief funds, and ensuring that financial integrity is upheld at every step."

As of Aug. 5, DePena had made only 16 payments toward the Tenares Tire EIDL, totaling $130,160. Since the payments went toward the accrued interest, the outstanding loan balance remains at approximately $1.65 million, the complaint states.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
DePena is scheduled to make his initial appearance in Boston federal court on Friday afternoon. He faces up to 30 years in prison.
The mayor's office did not immediately respond to Fox News Digital's request for comment.
Louis Casiano is a reporter for Fox News Digital. Story tips can be sent to louis.casiano@fox.com.

title: Exclusive: Israel seizes vast Iran terror axis arsenal with surprising foreign origins

story: Fox News Digital got rare access to rockets, drones, sniper rifles and other weapons seized from the terror groups, including Iranian-made arms. (Video: IDF.)

JERUSALEM — Fox News Digital gained rare access to the Israel Defense Forces (IDF) Tzrifin Base in Central Israel, where a vast number of confiscated rockets, grenades, drones, sniper rifles, automated weapons, anti-tank rocket launchers, mortars and other military firepower used by Hezbollah and Hamas are stored.

The seized arsenal of weapons, ranging in manufacturers from the Islamic Republic of Iran to Russia, China to homegrown producers in Lebanon and Gaza and even a Nazi-era gun, were part of the war machinery used by Hamas and Hezbollah against Israeli civilians and the IDF since Hamas terrorists attacked southern Israel on Oct. 7, 2023.
The IDF said Hezbollah also used weapons against Lebanese civilians.
Hezbollah and Hamas, members of Iran’s so-called "axis of resistance," have killed over 300 American citizens, according to reports.
'WE WANT LAND INVASION': IRAN MOUTHPIECE TOUTS NEW MISSILE, BOASTS DECADES OF WAR PREP
PK machine guns used by Hezbollah in Lebanon and seized by the IDF. (IDF)

The Jewish state fought a multi-front war against Iran and its proxies at the height of the conflict. The remains of Iranian rockets litter the ground outside the weapons storage facility at Tzrifin for journalists to inspect.

Tehran fired rockets into civilian areas during the war, including large cities such as Tel Aviv and Be’ersheva. Just days after the joint U.S.-Israeli attack on Iran in late February, the Islamic Republic fired a ballistic missile into Be’ersheva, causing injuries to 19 people.
To the ordinary eye, it is a Herculean challenge to decipher the small Nazi swastika emblem on the German World War II-era MG 34 machine gun seized at a Hezbollah terrorist compound in Lebanon.
But, for the Israeli military commander of the Captured Equipment Evacuation Unit, Lt. Col. (res.) Idan Sharon-Kettler, it is a run-of-the-mill exercise in weapons identification.
The German MG 34 has the "markings of an eagle carrying a swastika stamped on it," Sharon-Kettler said.

Hamas and Hezbollah, both of whom are designated terrorist organizations by the U.S., employed sophisticated methods to transform vehicles into high-intensity offensive weapons. Egyptian Halawa Motors motorcycles captured in Israel on Oct. 7. Motorcycles of this type were used to take hostages in Hamas-controlled Gaza. (IDF)
The IDF seized ATVs used by Hezbollah in Lebanon to hold rockets and terrorists. One captured ATV was designed to hold six rockets with launchers.
"You can sit on top of a hill and control a road that goes underneath. And with six anti-tank rockets, you will stop almost any vehicle that passes," Sharon-Kettler said.
He said the ATVs provide great utility for Hezbollah in the rugged, hilly landscape of southern Lebanon.

"We found hundreds" of mortars in Lebanon, Sharon-Kettler said. The IDF captured drones, including decay drones. Sharon-Kettler said some of the Hezbollah drones are used "to make noise … to divert [IDF]resources."
According to Sharon-Kettler, the IDF captured "dozens" of Iranian regime-produced canons in south Lebanese villages, where Hezbollah’s core base exists.

NETANYAHU REJECTS BOARD OF PEACE'S GAZA PLAN: NO 'WITHDRAWAL UNTIL HAMAS IS GENUINELY DISARMED'
Uniforms made in Syria, China and Lebanon and used by Hezbollah terrorists. (IDF)

Hezbollah, like its counterpart Hamas in Gaza, embeds its terrorists in residential areas and civilian buildings, including hospitals, schools and mosques. The IDF storage site was packed with Russian-produced AK-47 automatic rifles and various versions of it.
The IDF captured more recent Russian AK-103 and AK-104 automatic rifles in southern Lebanon.
"Light sniper rifles, some made in Iran, some Russian, are very common with Hezbollah and Hamas," Sharon-Kettler said.

Israel’s army also seized a highly decorated Turkish hunting rifle that was used by Hezbollah. The IDF found many highly sophisticated Austrian Steyr sniper rifles, including the Austrian Steyr HS .50 caliber sniper rifle, in possession of Hezbollah. Sharon-Kettler showed an Iranian replicated version of the Steyr sniper rifle.
The IDF collected submachine guns in Lebanon that were manufactured by China and Russia and anti-tank launchers produced by Russia and Iran, the IDF weapons expert said.

Additional merchandise seized by the IDF includes all the trappings of a professional army and guerrilla terrorist forces. Well-crafted uniforms made in Syria, China and Lebanon along with helmets, anti-shrapnel vests and medical kits are part of the IDF's confiscated war equipment.
Sharon-Kettler explained the reasons for Israel being in Lebanon.

"Even after the agreement we had with the Lebanese army and government, once we entered Lebanon again, we kept finding everything that is here. For me, it means, if we are not doing the work to clean Lebanon from military entities targeting are civilians, nobody else is doing that."
The IDF commander referred to the November 2024 ceasefire agreement reached between Lebanon and Israel to cease the war between Jerusalem and the Hezbollah terrorist organization.

A State Department official recently told Fox News the U.S.-led effort for Lebanon’s government to disarm Hezbollah and for a staged withdrawal of IDF troops from southern Lebanon will continue.

title: Spain stocks African enclave Ceuta with boosted security as Morocco monitors calls for second border rush
summary: Spain's African enclave Ceuta sees soldiers patrolling streets, and Morocco says it arrested those inciting a second mass border crossing on Saturday.
story: Fox News correspondent Stephanie Bennett reports on the political repercussions of migrants storming the Spanish enclave of Ceuta on ‘Fox Report.’

Spain and Morocco have beefed up security on both sides of the border in Spain's African enclave, Ceuta, as renewed calls circulate social media for Moroccan migrants to rush the border a second time after an initial mass migration event in July overwhelmed the city.
Soldiers patrolled the city's commercial and government buildings Friday while an enhanced police presence was noticeable on Ceuta's main avenues, Reuters reported.

On the Moroccan side, security personnel dressed in all-black patrolled the beaches of Fnideq, one of the most prominent launching points from which migrants illegally entered Ceuta on July 30 as part of a mass migration event that saw over 70,000 people rush into Ceuta from Morocco.
The strengthened security followed calls on social media for Moroccans to again rush into Ceuta and into Spain's other African enclave, Melilla, on Saturday.
FIREBRAND REP UNLOADS ON SOCIALIST PRIME MINISTER AS 'HORDES OF MILITARY AGED MEN' SWARM EUROPEAN COUNTRY

Moroccan security forces clash with migrants attempting to cross into Spain's North African enclave of Ceuta near the town of Fnideq on the Morocco-Spain border July 31, 2026. (Abdel Majid Bziouat/AFP via Getty Images)

"The Ministry of the Interior has detected, during the last few days, the circulation of anonymous publications and messages on certain social networks inciting the organization of attempts at collective and illegal crossing to the cities of Ceuta and Melilla, practices which carry serious risks to the safety of people and aim to instrumentalize migration issues in acts of incitement, which are criminalized by law," Morocco's Ministry of the Interior said in a statement posted to the country's state-affiliated news website MAP.
Morocco arrested multiple people who circulated the inciting statements, Interior Ministry spokesperson Rachid El Khalfi said.
The Interior Ministry also called on Spain to continue working to return the remaining Moroccan migrants in Ceuta back to the North African country.
TRUMP PUTS ASYLUM LAWYERS ‘ON NOTICE’ WITH NEW FRONT IN WAR ON FRAUD

Migrants run and cheer as they cross on foot into the North African enclave of Ceuta from Morocco after swimming over from the Moroccan side and overwhelming police at the city's breakwater, according to Spain's Guardia Civil, in Ceuta, Spain, July 30, 2026. (Faro TV via Reuters)

Of the more than 72,000 migrants who rushed the border, the vast majority have returned to Morocco, according to statements from Spain and Ceuta's government. About 5,000 remain, Spain's Interior Minister Fernando Grande-Marlaska told reporters Friday.
Spanish officials have been screening the remaining migrants and have processed roughly 500 asylum seekers' cases, rejecting the vast majority of them, Reuters reported.
Spain has also installed floating barriers in the waters migrants had previously swam across.

Members of the Royal Moroccan Navy patrol on the Moroccan side of the floating barrier off the border with Morocco after mass crossings of migrants on foot and by sea from Morocco into Spanish territory, as seen from Ceuta, Spain, Aug. 2, 2026. (Reuters/Violeta Santos Moura/File Photo)

At least 96 people died during the mass migration.

title: Iran jails psychologist over Trump plea as regime demands he make Americans ‘look stupid’: family
summary: Seyed Ahmad Seyedabdollahi was sentenced to seven months in prison by the Islamic Republic after posting a video appealing to Trump to support protesters.
story: Seyed Ahmad Seyedabdollahi, a 32-year-old Iranian psychologist, urges Trump to follow through on his pledge to support protesters. Arrested 10 days later, he was sentenced to seven months in prison. (Credit: Instagram/Seyed Ahmad Seyedabdollahi)

FIRST ON FOX: An Iranian psychologist who publicly appealed to President Donald Trump to stand by Iranians protesting the Islamic Republic has been sentenced to seven months in prison, while his relatives say authorities tried to pressure him into recording a video insulting Trump and Americans.

Seyed Ahmad Seyedabdollahi, a 32-year-old psychologist and counselor from Borujen who had been living in Tehran, posted an English-language video on Jan. 4 directly addressing Trump. In the video, reviewed by Fox News Digital, he urged the president to act quickly on his pledge to support Iranian protesters, saying young Iranians had trusted his words and that those who helped the Iranian people would be remembered.

""...To prove your good intentions to the Iranian people, either do something without saying anything or act very quickly on your words, because many young people trust what you say. And, as you probably know, many things are useless to people who are dead.I assure you that the Iranian nation remembers good deeds well, and they will try to repay their friends in the future."
TRUMP ADMIN BYPASSES TEHRAN'S ISOLATION CAMPAIGN TO REACH IRANIANS DIRECTLY

Seyed Ahmad Seyedabdollahi, a 32-year-old Iranian psychologist, who addressed President Donald Trump in an English-language video posted on Jan. 4, 2026, urging him to follow through on his pledge to support Iranian protesters. Seyedabdollahi was arrested 10 days later and was subsequently sentenced to seven months in prison. (Fox News)

Ten days later, on Jan. 14, Seyedabdollahi was arrested at his father's home in Borujen, according to Iran International, Iran Wire, Harana human rights activist news agency, and the Hana Human Rights Organization. Hana reported that plainclothes agents confiscated phones and electronic equipment and that Seyedabdollahi was subsequently held in solitary confinement and at an Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps intelligence detention facility in Isfahan.
A relative of Seyedabdollahi told Fox News Digital that the video triggered sustained pressure from Iranian security authorities.

"Since that day, he has faced serious pressure from Iranian security authorities. He was arrested twice and subjected to repeated interrogations," the relative said. "During his detention, he spent extended periods in solitary confinement. He was eventually convicted and sentenced to seven months in prison, and in July 2026 he was transferred to prison to begin serving his sentence."

Branch One of the Borujen Revolutionary Court convicted Seyedabdollahi of "engaging in media activities against national security," sentenced him to seven months in prison and barred him from government and public services for five years, Iran International reported Aug. 6. He was detained again July 7 to begin serving the sentence and remains in Borujen Prison.
IRAN INMATES SEW LIPS SHUT IN MASS HUNGER STRIKE AT NOTORIOUS US-SANCTIONED JAIL: REPORT
Iranians gather while blocking a street during a protest in Kermanshah, Iran on Jan. 8, 2026. (Kamran/Middle East Images/AFP via Getty Images)

Hana Human Rights Organization said he was denied contact with his family for 17 days following his first arrest and that his family initially did not know where he was being held. Iran International reported that he was denied access to a lawyer of his choosing during his detention and at times was prevented from communicating with his family.

Iranian authorities have also opened a second case against Seyedabdollahi on a charge translated as "propaganda against the establishment" or "propaganda against the system of the Islamic Republic." The case, opened in June, remains at the preliminary investigative stage, according to Hana.

Court documents obtained by Fox News Digital appear to detail the authorities' investigation of Seyedabdollahi and contain references to alleged foreign contacts and financial transactions involving the United States and Israel. His relative said interrogators accused him of being connected to the CIA and Mossad and of receiving money in exchange for making the video.
"They told him you are a member of the CIA and Mossad and you took money from them for this job," the relative said.
AIR FORCE INTEL VET ALLEGEDLY SPIRALED INTO IRAN’S TERROR UNDERWORLD: TIMELINE OF DECEIT, HUNT FOR SPY SUSPECT

Seyed Ahmad Seyedabdollahi, a 32-year-old Iranian psychologist, addresses President Donald Trump in an English-language video posted on Jan. 4, 2026, urging him to follow through on his pledge to support Iranian protesters. Seyedabdollahi was arrested 10 days later and was subsequently sentenced to seven months in prison. (Fox News)
The relative also alleged that Iranian authorities pressured Seyedabdollahi to record another video repudiating his original message and attacking Trump and Americans.

"He did not give in to numerous pressures to publish a clip that contradicted the first video," the relative said. "He was asked to sexually insult Trump and make the American people look stupid and ignorant so that we could broadcast your clip on the national media."

The relative further alleged that Seyedabdollahi endured solitary confinement and mistreatment during interrogations, and said he continues to face pressure in prison after refusing authorities' demands. Those allegations also could not be independently verified.

"His situation in Borujen Prison is not good because he has been out of solitary confinement for a few days, but sometimes they take him to solitary confinement under various pretexts," the relative said, adding that monitored telephone calls make it difficult for him to speak openly about his treatment.
FREED AMERICAN REVEALS BRUTAL IRAN PRISON ORDEAL, WARNS HOSTAGES FACE GREATER DANGER
Protesters chant slogans during a protest over the death of a woman who was detained by the morality police, in downtown Tehran, Iran. (AP Photo) (Associated Press)
The relative said the five-year prohibition on public and government employment has compounded the punishment by threatening Seyedabdollahi's ability to work after his release.
"You understand the economic conditions of Iran. Now imagine that in this situation someone has been deprived of their social rights, i.e. job and income, and he is imprisoned," the relative said.

The relative described Seyedabdollahi as a psychologist and popular speaker with a following among young Iranians, and said he remained focused on those who suffered more severely during the government's crackdown.
In the brief period when he was free, the relative recalled him saying, "Don't feel weak. Our problems are insignificant compared to the thousands of people who have lost their lives."

Seyedabdollahi was one of several Iranians who directly appealed to Trump during January's nationwide protests. Iran International reported that he posted his video Jan. 4, two days after Trump warned Iranian authorities against firing on peaceful demonstrators. Trump again warned Tehran on Jan. 9 and on Jan. 13 urged Iranians to continue protesting, writing that "help is on its way."
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

People gather during protest on January 8, 2026, in Tehran, Iran. Demonstrations have been ongoing since December, triggered by soaring inflation and the collapse of the rial, and have expanded into broader demands for political change. (Anonymous/Getty Images)

Iran International reported that the crackdown resulted in mass arrests and cited the U.S.-based Human Rights Activists News Agency as saying more than 50,000 people were arrested during a period of just over six weeks. The outlet also reported that U.N. human rights chief Volker Türk said at least 56 people had been executed on national-security-related charges since March 19, including 27 in cases linked to the January protests.
The Iranian mission to the U.N. declined to comment.

Lachter’s reporting has taken her into conflict zones and crisis areas across the Middle East, Europe, Asia and Africa. Her work has included uncovering human trafficking networks, revealing an ISIS underground torture prison in Syria, documenting the war in Ukraine and interviewing senior political figures and world leaders. She was also among the Western journalists who entered Russia after the war began to bring testimonies from Putin’s opposition. Lachter is the recipient of the 2022 Peres Center for Peace Award and was a 2023–2024 Knight-Wallace Journalism Fellow at the University of Michigan. She also won two Rockower Awards for Excellence in Reporting. She holds a bachelor's degree in communication and a master's degree in political science.

title: Construction workers uncover $10 million in gold while building sewer under former brewery
summary: Construction workers in Belgium discovered $10 million in gold coins and bars while building a sewer, but a finder's fee remains uncertain.
story: Matt Paxton tells Fox News Digital Season 2 uncovered gold coins, cash and homes worth hundreds of thousands, calling his discoveries some of the largest hoards of his career.
Construction workers in Belgium this week uncovered $10.4 million in gold while building a new sewer below a former brewery, according to local police.

Police in Sint-Gillis-Dendermonde, a Flemish community outside Brussels, said the workers contacted them immediately about the find, which officers cataloged, then placed in a "high-security federal government vault."
An 18-year-old worker on the site named Kobe told VRT news he at first thought the gold pieces were 1 Euro coins.

"Our first reaction was actually disbelief, surprise. Of course, we didn't expect to find gold," Kobe said, adding that the workers had to remove a piece of foundation to lay down pipe for the sewerage.
TREASURE HUNTERS STRIKE GOLD AFTER YEARS OF DISAPPOINTMENT WITH FIND WORTH A FORTUNE
Construction workers in Belgium this week uncovered $10.4 million in gold while building a new sewer below a former brewery, according to local police. (Lokale Politie Dendermonde/Facebook)
"When we did that, we suddenly saw something lying around," he said.
Project leader Mario said it was a "crazy feeling."

"They shouted, 'We found gold,'" he told the outlet of his workers. "I went to look and took the gold in my hands. We also continued to dig up new coins and bars. Only then did what we had found really dawn."
He called his boss and then the police.

Police in Sint-Gillis-Dendermonde, a Flemish community outside of Brussels, said the workers contacted them immediately about the find, which officers cataloged, then placed in a "high-security federal government vault." (Lokale Politie Dendermonde/Facebook)
The construction workers don’t actually get to keep the gold. Under Belgian law, the rightful owner has the right to claim the gold within five years.
When asked if it had crossed his mind to keep it, Mario told VRT, "It's about so many coins and bars, that almost wouldn't be possible. Besides, it would also be theft."
METAL DETECTORIST'S 'FEELING' LEADS TO MASSIVE ROMAN SETTLEMENT DISCOVERY IN POPULAR TOURIST HOTSPOT
Kobe said he still hoped for a finder’s fee. "That would be nice."
Police catalog the gold found in Belgium. (Lokale Politie Dendermonde/Facebook)
The building is owned by an organization that provides welfare support to the Flemish community.
The director of the organization said he hoped the gold could be used to help with the "enormous need we experience daily," according to the BBC.
